knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static directed capacitated networks with designated source and sink nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a directed graph \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\), capacities \(u_{ij}\in[0,\infty]\) for every \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\), and designated source and sink nodes \(s,t\), the maximum-flow problem is to maximize the value of a feasible \(s\)-to-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a directed network with nonnegative, possibly infinite arc capacities and designated source and sink nodes, the maximum-flow problem seeks a feasible source-to-sink flow of greatest value.
assumptions_latex: s,t\in\mathcal N\text{ are the designated source and sink}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{\operatorname{val}(f):f\text{ is a feasible }s\text{-}t\text{ flow respecting the arc capacities}\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows infinite edge capacities and characterizes the excluded unbounded case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacitated digraph with source $s$ and sink $t$, there is no $st$-path consisting entirely of edges of infinite capacity if and only if there exists an $s\bar t$-set $S$ with $\delta_g(S)<\infty$. An all-infinite-capacity $st$-path permits feasible flows of arbitrarily large value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There is no source-to-sink path made entirely of infinite-capacity edges exactly when some source-side cut has finite capacity. If such an all-infinite path exists, the flow value is unbounded.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a capacitated digraph with source }s\text{ and sink }t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\nexists\text{ all-infinite-capacity }st\text{-path}\right)\iff\left(\exists S:\ s\in S\subseteq V\setminus\{t\},\ \delta_g(S)<\infty\right),\quad \text{and such a path implies }\sup\{|x|:x\text{ feasible}\}=\infty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow-relative saturation and zero-flow status of a capacitated arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a flow \(f\) and an arc \((x,y)\) with capacity \(c(x,y)\), the arc is saturated with respect to \(f\) if \(f(x,y)=c(x,y)\), and it is flowless with respect to \(f\) if \(f(x,y)=0\). If the arc is both saturated and flowless, then \(c(x,y)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is saturated when its flow equals its capacity and flowless when its flow is zero. An arc having both statuses must have zero capacity.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a flow in a capacitated network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{saturated}_f(x,y)\iff f(x,y)=c(x,y),\quad \operatorname{flowless}_f(x,y)\iff f(x,y)=0,\quad \operatorname{saturated}_f(x,y)\land\operatorname{flowless}_f(x,y)\Rightarrow c(x,y)=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum feasible flow value with lower bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower- and upper-bounded source–sink flow duality, conditional on feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose there exists an \(s\)-\(t\) flow satisfying flow conservation and arc bounds \(\ell(x,y)\le f(x,y)\le c(x,y)\) with value \(v\). Then
\[
\min v=\max_{\substack{X\subseteq N\\s\in X,\ t\notin X}}\bigl(\ell(X,\bar X)-c(\bar X,X)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the lower- and upper-bounded source–sink flow constraints are feasible, the smallest feasible flow value equals the maximum, over source–sink cuts, of forward lower-bound demand minus reverse upper capacity.
assumptions_latex: X\subseteq N,\ s\in X,\ t\in\bar X.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min v=\max_{X:\,s\in X,\,t\in\bar X}\left[\ell(X,\bar X)-c(\bar X,X)\right].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: s–t Flow over Time with Intermediate Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time feasible-flow definition for a network with transit times and a fixed horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,s,t)$ be a network, let $l:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+$ assign transit times, and let $T\in\mathbb{R}_+$. An $s$–$t$ flow over time consists of Lebesgue-measurable functions $f_e:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}_+$ satisfying $f_e(\tau)\le u(e)$ for every $e\in E(G)$ and $\tau\in[0,T]$, and, for every $v\in V(G)\setminus\{s\}$ and $a\in[0,T]$, $$\operatorname{ex}_f(v,a):=\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}\int_0^{\max\{0,a-l(e)\}}f_e(\tau)\,d\tau-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}\int_0^a f_e(\tau)\,d\tau\ge0.$$ The value $f_e(\tau)$ is the rate entering $e$ at time $\tau$ and leaving it $l(e)$ time units later; the excess condition permits storage at intermediate vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s–t flow over time assigns each edge a nonnegative measurable entry rate bounded by its capacity. At every time and every vertex other than the source, cumulative arrived flow must be at least cumulative departed flow, allowing intermediate storage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is an }s\text{–}t\text{ flow over time when it satisfies the stated measurability, capacity, and cumulative-excess conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse decomposition of an arbitrary source-to-sink flow, with integral weights when the flow is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,s,t)$ be a network and let $f$ be an $s$-$t$ flow in $G$. There exist a family $\mathcal P$ of $s$-$t$ paths, a family $\mathcal C$ of circuits, and weights $w:\mathcal P\cup\mathcal C\to\mathbb R_+$ such that, for every $e\in E(G)$, $f(e)=\sum_{Q\in\mathcal P\cup\mathcal C:\,e\in E(Q)}w(Q)$, while $\sum_{P\in\mathcal P}w(P)=\operatorname{value}(f)$ and $|\mathcal P|+|\mathcal C|\le |E(G)|$. Moreover, if $f$ is integral, then $w$ can be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every source-to-sink flow is a nonnegative weighted sum of source-to-sink paths and circuits using at most as many components as the graph has edges. The total path weight equals the flow value, and an integral flow admits integral component weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\mathcal P,\mathcal C,w:\ f(e)=\sum_{Q\ni e}w(Q)\ (\forall e),\quad \sum_{P\in\mathcal P}w(P)=\operatorname{value}(f),\quad |\mathcal P|+|\mathcal C|\le |E(G)|;\quad f\text{ integral}\Rightarrow w\text{ may be integral}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equation-node and variable-arc correspondence, including the converse extension using omitted diagonal variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the transshipment equations $\sum_i x_{ik}-\sum_j x_{kj}=a_k-b_k$, map equation $k$ to node $k$ and every admissible off-diagonal variable $x_{ij}$ to the directed arc $i\to j$. The equation at node $k$ is equivalently $\sum_i x_{ik}+a_k=\sum_j x_{kj}+b_k$. Thus every solution of the equations has a corresponding arc assignment satisfying these node balances. Conversely, any arc assignment satisfying all such balances extends to a solution of the equation system by assigning each omitted diagonal variable the common incoming and outgoing total. Feasibility additionally requires the prescribed nonnegativity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each transshipment equation is represented by a node and each admissible shipment variable by a directed arc. The algebraic equation becomes equality of total incoming flow plus availability and total outgoing flow plus requirement. Every equation-system solution gives such a balanced network assignment, and every balanced assignment extends to a solution by setting omitted diagonal variables to the common node total. Nonnegativity remains a separate feasibility requirement.
assumptions_latex: x_{ij}\text{ is represented only when }(i,j)\text{ is admissible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Solutions of the transshipment equations correspond to balanced directed-network assignments, with the stated diagonal-variable extension.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applicability of the elementary directed-network transformation for undirected shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An undirected shortest-path instance whose edge lengths are all nonnegative can be transformed into a directed-network instance. The elementary transformation does not apply when an undirected edge has negative length, because that edge produces a negative directed cycle; a different transformation is then required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected shortest-path problem with nonnegative lengths can be transformed into a directed problem. The elementary transformation fails for a negative edge because it creates a negative directed cycle, so another transformation is needed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph, directed arc, chain, loop, tree, and end
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For chains, loops, and trees, connectivity is evaluated without regard to arc orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network consists of nodes and arcs, each arc joining two nodes. A directed arc $i\to j$ records an allowed orientation; distinct parallel arcs and oppositely directed arcs remain distinct. A chain from $i$ to $j$ is a sequence $(i,i_1),(i_1,i_2),\ldots,(i_k,j)$ without regard to the arcs' directions. A loop is a chain from a node to itself and is simple when its arcs are distinct. A tree is a graph containing no loop in which every pair of nodes is connected by a chain. An end is a node joined to the network by exactly one arc. A crossing of drawn arcs is not an incidence unless it occurs at a node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network has nodes joined by arcs, with directed arcs retaining their orientations and distinct arcs remaining distinct. Ignoring orientation, a chain connects two nodes, a loop is a closed chain, a tree is loop-free and connected by chains, and an end has exactly one incident arc. Crossings in a drawing are not nodes unless explicitly marked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These clauses define the stated elementary network objects.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and existence characterization for finite directed networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a finite directed network with \(|N|=n\). A topological ordering is a bijection \(\operatorname{order}:N\to\{1,\ldots,n\}\) such that \(\operatorname{order}(i)<\operatorname{order}(j)\) for every \((i,j)\in A\). Such an ordering exists if and only if \(G\) contains no directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological ordering labels the vertices distinctly from 1 through n so that every arc points from a lower label to a higher label. A finite directed network admits such an ordering exactly when it is acyclic.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a finite directed network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ has a topological ordering}\iff G\text{ contains no directed cycle}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines elementary nonnegative flows supported on one directed path or circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a directed \(st\)-path and \(C\) a directed circuit in \(D=(V,A)\). For \(\alpha\ge 0\), define \(x_1(e)=\alpha\) for \(e\in P\) and \(0\) otherwise, and define \(x_2(e)=\alpha\) for \(e\in C\) and \(0\) otherwise. Then \(x_1\) is a path-flow and \(x_2\) is a cycle-flow, hence respectively an \(st\)-flow and a circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assigning the same nonnegative value to every arc of a directed source-to-sink path and zero elsewhere gives a path-flow. Doing the same on a directed circuit gives a cycle-flow, which is a circulation.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a directed circuit in }D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_1\text{ is a path-flow and an }st\text{-flow, while }x_2\text{ is a cycle-flow and a circulation}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Chains, Orientation-Relaxed Paths, and Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source convention in which a chain follows arc orientations, whereas a path may traverse an arc against its orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 2\), let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be distinct nodes. If \((x_i,x_{i+1})\in\alpha\) for every \(i=1,\ldots,n-1\), the associated node–arc sequence is a directed chain from \(x_1\) to \(x_n\). If instead, for each \(i\), one selects an arc joining \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) in either orientation, the resulting sequence is a path; the selected arc is forward when traversed in its orientation and reverse otherwise. In each definition, replacing distinctness of all nodes by \(x_n=x_1\) with the remaining nodes distinct gives the corresponding closed object, called respectively a directed cycle or a cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed chain follows every selected arc in its orientation. Under the source convention, a path may traverse selected arcs either with or against their orientation, producing forward and reverse arcs. Closing the corresponding sequence gives a directed cycle or a cycle.
assumptions_latex: \text{For open chains and paths, }x_1,\ldots,x_n\text{ are distinct}
\text{For closed variants, }x_n=x_1\text{ and the other nodes retain the intended distinctness}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall i,\ (x_i,x_{i+1})\in\alpha\bigr]\Rightarrow\text{directed chain};\qquad \bigl[\forall i,\ (x_i,x_{i+1})\in\alpha\lor(x_{i+1},x_i)\in\alpha\bigr]\Rightarrow\text{path after selecting one joining arc per step}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual network of a feasible flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines residual arcs copy-by-copy, allowing multiple copies when antiparallel original arcs generate the same ordered residual arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a capacitated network \(N=(s,t,V,A,b)\) and a feasible flow \(f\), the residual network \(N(f)=(s,t,V,A(f),ac)\) is formed as follows. For each \((u,v)\in A\), if \(f(u,v)<b(u,v)\), add a forward residual arc \((u,v)\) with \(ac(u,v)=b(u,v)-f(u,v)\); if \(f(u,v)>0\), add a reverse residual arc \((v,u)\) with \(ac(v,u)=f(u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each original arc, the residual network contains a forward copy carrying unused capacity when the arc is not saturated and a reverse copy carrying the current flow when that flow is positive.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a feasible flow in }N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall (u,v)\in A:\quad f(u,v)<b(u,v)\Rightarrow (u,v)\in A(f),\ ac(u,v)=b(u,v)-f(u,v),\quad f(u,v)>0\Rightarrow (v,u)\in A(f),\ ac(v,u)=f(u,v).

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Walk Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed walks, allowing repeated vertices and arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph with tail and head maps \(\tau,\eta:A\to V\). A directed walk of length \(k\ge 0\) is an alternating sequence \(W=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) such that \(\tau(a_i)=v_{i-1}\) and \(\eta(a_i)=v_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). Its initial vertex is \(v_0\), its terminal vertex is \(v_k\), and it is closed when \(v_0=v_k\). Vertices and arcs may repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed walk is a finite, direction-respecting sequence of incident vertices and arcs; repetitions are allowed, and the walk is closed when its endpoints coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) is a directed walk exactly when \(\tau(a_i)=v_{i-1}\) and \(\eta(a_i)=v_i\) for all \(i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed graphs, weak connectivity, and directed traversal objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the convention that an undirected-style walk may traverse a directed arc forward or backward, whereas a directed walk uses only forward arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed graph is \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\), where every arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\) is an ordered pair of distinct nodes; both \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) may occur, but \((i,i)\) may not. For \(i\in\mathcal N\), \(I(i)=\{j\in\mathcal N:(j,i)\in\mathcal A\}\) and \(O(i)=\{j\in\mathcal N:(i,j)\in\mathcal A\}\). The graph is connected when the simple undirected graph obtained by forgetting arc directions and merging opposite arcs is connected. A walk consists of nodes \(i_1,\ldots,i_t\) and arcs \(a_1,\ldots,a_{t-1}\) such that each \(a_k\) equals either \((i_k,i_{k+1})\), a forward arc, or \((i_{k+1},i_k)\), a backward arc. A path has all nodes distinct. A cycle has \(i_1,\ldots,i_{t-1}\) distinct and \(i_t=i_1\), and may contain only two distinct nodes. A walk, path, or cycle is directed exactly when every traversed arc is forward.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loopless directed graph has ordered arcs and may contain both orientations between two nodes. Its in- and out-neighborhoods record incoming start nodes and outgoing end nodes. Connectivity means connectivity after directions are forgotten. Under the stated convention, a walk records which arc is used and may traverse it forward or backward; paths have distinct nodes, cycles return to their start and may use two distinct nodes, and a traversal is directed only when all arcs are forward.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W\text{ is directed}\iff \text{every arc used by }W\text{ is forward}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed walks and their path and circuit specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers orientation-respecting walks, simple directed paths, reachability, length, concatenation, disjointness, and closed-walk and circuit conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a digraph D=(V,A), a directed walk is a sequence P=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k), where k\geq0 and a_i=(v_{i-1},v_i) for i=1,\ldots,k. It is a directed path if v_0,\ldots,v_k are distinct. A vertex t is reachable from s if a directed s-t path exists. The unweighted length of P is k; given l:A\to\mathbb{R}, its l-length is \sum_{i=1}^k l(a_i), and the distance from u to v is the minimum length of a u-v path. Walks with the last vertex of the first equal to the first vertex of the second may be concatenated. Two walks are vertex-disjoint, internally vertex-disjoint, or arc-disjoint when their respective vertex sets, internal-vertex sets, or arc families are disjoint. A directed walk is closed when v_k=v_0 and is a directed circuit when additionally k\geq1, v_1,\ldots,v_k are distinct, and a_1,\ldots,a_k are distinct.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed walk follows the orientations of its arcs. It is a directed path when it repeats no vertex, and reachability means that such a path exists. Length is the number of arcs unless an arc-length function is specified. Compatible walks can be concatenated, disjointness can concern vertices, internal vertices, or arcs, and a circuit is a nonempty closed directed walk satisfying the stated distinctness conditions.
assumptions_latex: l:A\to\mathbb{R}\text{ when weighted length is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is a directed path}\iff v_0,\ldots,v_k\text{ are distinct},\qquad t\text{ is reachable from }s\iff\exists\text{ a directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Path Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite simple directed paths, including the zero-length path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) is a directed walk \(P=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) with \(v_0=s\), \(v_k=t\), and pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\). Consequently its arcs are also distinct. The case \(k=0\) is permitted and gives the path consisting of the single vertex \(s=t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed path is a direction-respecting walk with no repeated vertex; a single vertex is admitted as a path of length zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a directed \(s\)-\(t\) path exactly when it is a directed walk from \(s\) to \(t\) whose vertices are pairwise distinct.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Blocking Sequence for an Exact Matroid Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a minimal sequence of ambient-matroid elements that locally obstructs the separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, let (X,Y) be an exact k-separation of N, and let (v_1,\ldots,v_t) be elements of E(M)\setminus E(N). It is a blocking sequence for (X,Y) with respect to D,C if: (a) (X,Y\cup\{v_1\}) is not a k-separation of M[D,C;\{v_1\}]; (b) (X\cup\{v_t\},Y) is not a k-separation of M[D,C;\{v_t\}]; (c) for every i\in\{1,\ldots,t-1\}, (X\cup\{v_i\},Y\cup\{v_{i+1}\}) is not a k-separation of M[D,C;\{v_i,v_{i+1}\}]; and no proper subsequence satisfies (a)--(c).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blocking sequence is a minimal sequence of elements outside N whose first element, last element, and every consecutive pair respectively prevent the indicated extensions of (X,Y) from being k-separations in the corresponding minors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (v_1,\ldots,v_t)\text{ is a blocking sequence exactly when conditions (a)--(c) hold and no proper subsequence satisfies them}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary Digraph for Detecting Blocking Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the obstruction digraph and the relevant subsequence-minimal notion of directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an exact k-separation (X,Y), define G(X,Y) with vertex set \{v_X,v_Y\}\cup(E(M)\setminus E(N)). Its arcs are: (v_X,w) whenever (X,Y\cup\{w\}) is not a k-separation of M[D,C;\{w\}]; (w,v_Y) whenever (X\cup\{w\},Y) is not a k-separation of M[D,C;\{w\}]; and (u,w), for distinct u,w\in E(M)\setminus E(N), whenever (X\cup\{u\},Y\cup\{w\}) is not a k-separation of M[D,C;\{u,w\}]. A directed path u,v_1,\ldots,v_r,v is minimal if no proper subsequence is also a directed (u,v)-path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary digraph has two terminal vertices and one vertex for every element outside N. Its arcs encode failure of the relevant one-element or two-element extensions to remain k-separations. A path is minimal when deleting any internal vertices cannot leave a directed path with the same endpoints.
assumptions_latex: (X,Y)\text{ is an exact }k\text{-separation in the matroid blocking-sequence setting}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G(X,Y)\text{ has the stated vertex and arc sets, and path minimality means subsequence-minimality among directed paths with fixed endpoints}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-terminal planar dual construction and path–cocycle correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the planarity boundary, terminal splitting construction, and correspondence for simple directed terminal paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ have designated terminals $s,t$, add a distinguished arc $e=(t,s)$, allowing $e$ to be parallel to an existing arc, and assume $G+e$ is planar. Form $(G+e)^D$ and orient $e^*$ from $s^*$ to $t^*$. Deleting $e^*$ yields a dual representation of $G$ in which the dual node of the face of $G$ containing $s$ and $t$ on its boundary is split into $s^*$ and $t^*$. If $C$ is a directed simple $s$-$t$ path in $G$, then $C+e$ is a directed cycle in $G+e$, and $C^*$ is a directed $(s^*,t^*)$-cocycle in $(G+e)^D-e^*$. A graph is $(s,t)$-planar precisely when adding $(t,s)$ preserves planarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add an arc from t to s and dualize the resulting planar graph, orienting the added dual arc from s* to t*. Removing that dual arc splits the old face vertex into the two dual terminals. Every simple directed s-to-t path then corresponds to a directed s*-to-t* cocycle. This construction is available exactly when adding the t-to-s arc leaves the graph planar.
assumptions_latex: e=(t,s)\text{ is added, possibly parallel to an existing arc.}
C\text{ is a directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path with no repeated nodes.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^*\text{ is a directed }(s^*,t^*)\text{-cocycle in }(G+e)^D-e^*;\qquad G\text{ is }(s,t)\text{-planar}\iff G+(t,s)\text{ is planar}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Label-and-scan construction of the reachable arborescence of a directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph D and root r, initialize r as labelled and no vertex as scanned. Repeatedly choose a labelled unscanned vertex v. If v has an outgoing line to an unlabelled vertex u, add that line to the rooted arborescence and label u; otherwise mark v scanned. Stop when every labelled vertex is scanned. The resulting arborescence contains exactly the vertices reachable from r by directed paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a labelled root, repeatedly discover an unlabelled out-neighbor of a labelled vertex, or mark the vertex scanned when none remains. When the process stops, its rooted arborescence contains exactly the vertices reachable from the root.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(A)=\{v\in V(D):\text{ there is a directed path from }r\text{ to }v\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete digraphs, tournaments, and line digraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines two simple directed-graph classes and the line-digraph construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The complete directed graph on V is the simple digraph with arc set \{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}. A tournament is a simple digraph (V,A) such that for every distinct u,v\in V, exactly one of (u,v) and (v,u) belongs to A. For D=(V,A), its line digraph has vertex set A and arc set \{((u,v),(x,y)):(u,v),(x,y)\in A,\ v=x\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete digraph contains both orientations between every two distinct vertices. A tournament selects exactly one orientation for each unordered pair. The line digraph represents arcs of the original digraph as vertices and joins two when the head of the first is the tail of the second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A(K_V^{\rightarrow})=\{(u,v):u,v\in V,\ u\ne v\},\qquad A(L(D))=\{(a,b)\in A^2:\operatorname{head}(a)=\operatorname{tail}(b)\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted dual form of the chain versus antichain-cover min–max theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((S,\preceq)\) be a finite partially ordered set and let \(w:S\to\mathbb Z_+\). Then
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{s\in C}w(s):C\subseteq S\text{ is a chain}\right\}
=
\min\left\{k:\begin{array}{l}A_1,\ldots,A_k\text{ are antichains, and each }s\in S\\
\text{belongs to exactly }w(s)\text{ of the }A_i\end{array}\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite poset with nonnegative integer element weights, the maximum total weight of a chain equals the minimum number of antichains, counted with multiplicity, needed so that every element s occurs in exactly w(s) antichains.
assumptions_latex: (S,\preceq)\text{ is a finite partially ordered set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{C\text{ chain}}\sum_{s\in C}w(s)=\min\{k:A_1,\ldots,A_k\text{ are antichains and }|\{i:s\in A_i\}|=w(s)\ \forall s\in S\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and predecessor representation, including its failure boundary for repeated-node walks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed path is a directed walk with no repeated nodes; equivalently, it is a path with no backward arcs. It may be represented by setting $\operatorname{pred}(j)=i$ when $i$ immediately precedes $j$ along the path, optionally using $\operatorname{pred}(s)=0$ for the initial node $s$. One predecessor index per node cannot in general encode a walk that revisits nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed path is an orientation-respecting walk without repeated nodes. It can be stored by recording each node's immediate predecessor, optionally assigning zero to the initial node. A single predecessor per node cannot generally encode repeated-node walks.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a directed walk in }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is a directed path}\iff P\text{ has no repeated nodes};\quad \operatorname{pred}(j)=i\text{ for consecutive }i,j\text{ on }P,\text{ while this representation is generally insufficient for repeated-node walks.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Paths, Dicircuits, and Path Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-path terminology and additive costs on directed paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E,t,h)\) be a finite digraph. In a path \(P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\), the arc \(e_i\) is forward when \(t(e_i)=v_{i-1}\) and \(h(e_i)=v_i\). A path in which every arc is forward is a dipath, and a dipath that is also a circuit is a dicircuit. If \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), then the cost of a dipath is \(c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^k c_{e_i}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed path follows every arc from its tail to its head, and a directed path that is a circuit is a dicircuit. With real arc costs, the cost of a directed path is the sum of its arc costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is a dipath iff }t(e_i)=v_{i-1},\ h(e_i)=v_i\ \forall i;\qquad c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^k c_{e_i}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path Telescoping and Cycle Invariance of Reduced Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential-adjusted costs on directed paths and cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any node potential \(\pi\), every directed path \(P\) from node \(k\) to node \(l\) satisfies \[\sum_{(i,j)\in P}c_{ij}^{\pi}=\sum_{(i,j)\in P}c_{ij}-\pi(k)+\pi(l).\] Consequently, every directed cycle \(W\) satisfies \[\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}^{\pi}=\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a directed path, potential adjustments telescope to the difference between the endpoint potentials. On a directed cycle, they cancel completely, so reduced cost and original cost have the same total.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is a set of node potentials and \(c_{ij}^{\pi}\) denotes the corresponding reduced arc cost.
\(P\) is a directed path from \(k\) to \(l\), or \(W\) is a directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{(i,j)\in P}c_{ij}^{\pi}=\sum_{(i,j)\in P}c_{ij}-\pi(k)+\pi(l),\qquad \sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}^{\pi}=\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for general directed graphs, including single-arc ears.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph. An ear of \(D\) is a directed path or directed circuit \(P\) such that every internal vertex of \(P\) has indegree and outdegree equal to \(1\) in \(D\); a single arc is permitted. If \(I\) is the set of internal vertices of \(P\), then adding \(P\) to \(D-I\) produces \(D\). An ear-decomposition of \(D\) is a sequence \(D_0,D_1,\ldots,D_k\) with \(D_0=K_1\), \(D_k=D\), and, for every \(i=1,\ldots,k\), \(D_i\) obtained from \(D_{i-1}\) by adding an ear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a digraph, an ear is a directed path or circuit whose internal vertices each have indegree and outdegree one in the whole digraph; a single arc may be an ear. An ear-decomposition builds the digraph from a one-vertex digraph by successively adding ears.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (D_0,\ldots,D_k)\text{ is an ear-decomposition of }D\iff D_0=K_1,\ D_k=D,\text{ and each }D_i\text{ arises from }D_{i-1}\text{ by adding an ear}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclic directed cut–path covering min-max theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A min-max identity for covering a selected arc set by at most k directed cuts versus leaving arcs uncovered by a path collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let D=(V,A) be an acyclic digraph, let B\subseteq A, and let k\in\mathbb Z_+. Then

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Walks, paths, cycles, reachability, and graph distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary structural properties for directed or undirected graphs, including edge-weighted variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be directed or undirected. An edge progression from \(v_1\) to \(v_{k+1}\) is a sequence \(v_1,e_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k,e_k,v_{k+1}\), with \(k\ge0\), in which each \(e_i\) joins \(v_i\) to \(v_{i+1}\) with the appropriate orientation in a digraph. It is a walk when its edges are pairwise distinct and is closed when \(v_1=v_{k+1}\). A path is such a walk with pairwise distinct vertices; its first and last vertices are its endpoints, and any two vertices \(x,y\) on it determine a unique subpath \(P_{[x,y]}\). An edge progression from \(v\) to \(w\) exists if and only if a \(v\)-\(w\) path exists; in an undirected graph this reachability relation is an equivalence relation. A circuit or cycle is a closed walk of length \(k\ge2\) whose cyclically listed vertices are pairwise distinct, and the edge set of every closed walk can be partitioned into edge sets of circuits. In a digraph, an undirected path or circuit means one in the underlying undirected graph. Path or circuit length is its number of edges; a spanning path is Hamiltonian, a spanning circuit is a Hamiltonian circuit or tour, and a graph containing one is Hamiltonian. Moreover, \[\operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\min\{|E(P)|:P\text{ is a }v\text{-}w\text{ path in }G\},\] with value \(\infty\) when no such path exists, and \(\operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\operatorname{dist}_G(w,v)\) for undirected \(G\). Given \(c:E(G)\to\mathbb R\), define \(c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c(e)\), including \(c(\varnothing)=0\); this is modular on \(2^{E(G)}\), and \[\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(v,w)=\min_{P\text{ a }v\text{-}w\text{ path}}c(E(P)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge progression follows consecutive directed arcs or undirected edges; it is called a walk here when it repeats no edge and is closed when its endpoints coincide. A path also repeats no vertex, and every two of its vertices determine a unique subpath. Progression reachability is equivalent to path reachability and, for undirected graphs, is an equivalence relation. A cycle is a vertex-simple closed walk of at least two edges, and every closed walk's edges partition into cycle edge sets. The packet also defines underlying-undirected paths and cycles in digraphs, Hamiltonian paths and tours, ordinary distance with infinity for unreachable pairs, symmetry in undirected graphs, modular edge-set cost, and minimum-cost path distance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a directed or undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\leadsto w\iff G\text{ contains a }v\text{-}w\text{ path};\quad \operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\infty\text{ if }w\text{ is unreachable from }v;\quad G\text{ undirected}\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}_G(v,w)=\operatorname{dist}_G(w,v),\text{ and every closed-walk edge set partitions into circuit edge sets.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circulation Covers and c-Independent Node Vectors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions used in weighted covering of a digraph by directed circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph in which every vertex belongs to a directed circuit, with $c:A\to\mathbb Z_+$ and $w:V\to\mathbb Z_+$. A nonnegative circulation $x$ covers $w$ if $\delta_x(u)\ge w(u)$ for every $u\in V$. For a directed circuit $K$, let $\widetilde c(K)=\sum_{e\in K}c(e)$. A vector $z:V\to\mathbb Z_+$ is $c$-independent if $\sum_{v\in V(K)}z(v)\le\widetilde c(K)$ for every directed circuit $K$ of $D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative circulation covers the vertex-weight vector when its flow incident outward at every vertex meets that vertex's demand. A nonnegative integral node-multiplicity vector is c-independent when, on every directed circuit, its total multiplicity is at most the total arc cost of that circuit.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph and every }v\in V\text{ belongs to a directed circuit}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ covers }w\iff \delta_x(u)\ge w(u)\ \forall u\in V;\qquad z\text{ is }c\text{-independent}\iff \sum_{v\in V(K)}z(v)\le\sum_{e\in K}c(e)\ \forall\text{ directed circuits }K.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed path search between vertex sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The working-set removal order is arbitrary; predecessor labels record the discovered path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph $D=(V,A)$ and sets $S,T\subseteq V$, assign label $0$ to every vertex in $S$ and return a one-vertex path immediately if $S\cap T\neq\varnothing$. Initialize $Q=S$. While $Q\neq\varnothing$, remove any $v\in Q$ and inspect every out-neighbor $v'\in A(v)$. If $v'$ is unlabeled, set $\operatorname{label}(v')=v$; if $v'\in T$, follow the predecessor labels recursively to return a directed path from some vertex of $S$ to $v'$, and otherwise add $v'$ to $Q$. If $Q$ is exhausted, report that no directed path from $S$ to $T$ exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label all source-set vertices and explore their outgoing arcs. Each newly reached vertex stores its predecessor. If the target set is reached, following predecessor labels returns a directed path from S to T; if exploration ends first, the algorithm reports that no such path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The algorithm returns a directed path from some }s\in S\text{ to some }t\in T\text{ if one exists, and otherwise reports that none exists}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simple directed cycles represented with a distinguished starting position.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A directed cycle of length \(k\ge 1\) is a closed directed walk \(C=(v_0,a_1,v_1,\ldots,a_k,v_k)\) satisfying \(v_k=v_0\) and having pairwise distinct vertices \(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\). Thus each arc is traversed in its prescribed direction and no vertex repeats except the common initial-terminal vertex. Cyclic rotations represent the same unrooted cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed cycle is a nonempty closed directed walk with no repeated vertex apart from its coincident first and last vertex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the linear-time predecessor-graph test, its amortized scheduling, and the label-threshold recovery condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Mark the source and leave all other nodes unmarked. For each unmarked node \(k\), mark \(k\), follow predecessor indices while marking newly encountered nodes, and stop at the first previously marked node \(l\). If \(k=l\), the predecessor graph contains a directed cycle, and that cycle is negative. The full test takes \(O(n)\) time; performing it after every \(\alpha n\) distance updates, for constant \(\alpha>0\), does not increase the worst-case asymptotic complexity of a label-correcting algorithm. Moreover, if predecessor arcs satisfy \(d(j)\ge d(i)+c_{ij}\) whenever \(\operatorname{pred}(j)=i\), then a node \(j\) with \(d(j)\le -nC\) cannot be connected to the source by a predecessor path, so tracing predecessors from \(j\) reaches a negative cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A predecessor graph can be checked for cycles in linear time by marking nodes while tracing predecessor chains. A chain returning to its starting node identifies a negative cycle. Running this check every constant multiple of n label updates preserves the label-correcting algorithm's worst-case asymptotic complexity. A label at most -nC also forces its predecessor chain to enter a negative cycle under the stated predecessor-label inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \text{Every predecessor-graph directed cycle arising in this computation is negative}.
\text{Any source-rooted predecessor path has length at least }-nC\text{ under the stated bound.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The predecessor graph can be tested in }O(n)\text{ time, and }d(j)\le -nC\implies\text{ predecessor tracing from }j\text{ reaches a negative cycle.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W\) be a cycle from a specified node \(s\) to itself with a fixed orientation, and let \(\bar W\) and \(\underline W\) denote its forward and backward arcs. Define \[\mu(W)=\frac{\prod_{(i,j)\in\bar W}\mu_{ij}}{\prod_{(i,j)\in\underline W}\mu_{ij}}.\] Sending one unit around \(W\) from \(s\) returns \(\mu(W)\) units to \(s\). The cycle is gainy if \(\mu(W)>1\), lossy if \(\mu(W)<1\), and breakeven if \(\mu(W)=1\). In the breakeven case, flow around the cycle preserves mass balance at every node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oriented cycle's multiplier is the product of forward-arc gains divided by the product of backward-arc gains. One unit sent around it returns the multiplier amount. Multipliers above, below, and equal to one define gainy, lossy, and breakeven cycles; breakeven flow preserves mass balance at every node.
assumptions_latex: W\text{ is a cycle from }s\text{ to itself with a fixed orientation}
\bar W\text{ and }\underline W\text{ are its forward and backward arcs relative to that orientation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu(W)=\frac{\prod_{(i,j)\in\bar W}\mu_{ij}}{\prod_{(i,j)\in\underline W}\mu_{ij}},\quad 1\mapsto\mu(W),\quad \mu(W)>1\text{ is gainy},\ \mu(W)<1\text{ is lossy},\ \mu(W)=1\text{ is breakeven}

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Cut Objects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outgoing and incoming arc boundaries of a vertex subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph and let \(S\subseteq V\). The outgoing and incoming directed boundaries of \(S\) are \[\delta^+(S)=\{a\in A:\tau(a)\in S,\ \eta(a)\in V\setminus S\},\qquad \delta^-(S)=\{a\in A:\tau(a)\in V\setminus S,\ \eta(a)\in S\}.\] If distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) satisfy \(s\in S\) and \(t\notin S\), then \(S\), the bipartition \((S,V\setminus S)\), or the outgoing boundary \(\delta^+(S)\) is called a directed \(s\)-\(t\) cut, according to context.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The outgoing and incoming boundaries of a vertex subset consist of the arcs crossing its induced partition in the respective directions. An s–t cut has s in the selected subset and t outside it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta^+(S)\) contains exactly the arcs leaving \(S\), while \(\delta^-(S)\) contains exactly the arcs entering \(S\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and equivalent dijoin characterizations in an arbitrary digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$. A set $C\subseteq A$ is a dicut if $C=\delta_D^-(S)$ for some $\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V$ satisfying $\delta_D^+(S)=\varnothing$. A set $J\subseteq A$ is a dijoin if $J\cap C\ne\varnothing$ for every dicut $C$. Equivalently, $J$ is a dijoin if and only if adding the reverse arc $(v,u)$ for every $(u,v)\in J$ makes the resulting digraph strongly connected; equivalently, contracting the arcs in $J$ makes the resulting digraph strongly connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dicut consists of all arcs entering a nonempty proper vertex set from which no arc leaves. A dijoin is an arc set meeting every dicut. Equivalently, adding a reverse copy of every arc in the dijoin, or contracting all its arcs, makes the digraph strongly connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C=\delta_D^-(S),\ \varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V,\ \delta_D^+(S)=\varnothing\text{ defines a dicut, and }J\text{ is a dijoin exactly under each of the stated equivalent conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed source–sink cut objects and their elementary separating property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(N,A)\) be a directed network. If \(X\subseteq N\), \(\bar X=N\setminus X\), \(s\in X\), and \(t\in\bar X\), then the cut separating \(s\) from \(t\) is \[(X,\bar X)=\{(x,y)\in A:x\in X,\ y\in\bar X\},\] and its capacity is \(c(X,\bar X)\). Every directed \(s\)-to-\(t\) chain contains an arc of \((X,\bar X)\); consequently, deleting every arc in the cut eliminates all such chains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A source–sink cut is the set of arcs leaving a vertex set that contains the source but not the sink. Every directed source-to-sink chain crosses the cut, so deleting all its arcs eliminates every such chain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed boundary notation, cut variants, disconnecting arc sets, and the one-way minimal-disconnector characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph. For $U\subseteq V$, $\delta_D^{\mathrm{in}}(U)$ and $\delta_D^{\mathrm{out}}(U)$ are respectively the arcs entering and leaving $U$, with $d_D^{\mathrm{in}}(U)=|\delta_D^{\mathrm{in}}(U)|$ and $d_D^{\mathrm{out}}(U)=|\delta_D^{\mathrm{out}}(U)|$. A cut is a set $\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(U)$; it is nontrivial if $\varnothing
e U
e V$, an $s$-$t$ cut if $s\in U$ and $t
otin U$, and an $S$-$T$ cut if $S\subseteq U$ and $T\subseteq V\setminus U$. A set $B\subseteq A$ is disconnecting if $D-B$ is not strongly connected; it is $s$-$t$ disconnecting if it meets every directed $s$-$t$ path, and analogously for $S$-$T$. Every $s$-$t$ cut is $s$-$t$ disconnecting, and every inclusionwise minimal $s$-$t$ disconnecting arc set is an $s$-$t$ cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entering and leaving boundaries contain the arcs entering and leaving a vertex set, and their cardinalities are its in- and out-boundary degrees. A cut is a leaving boundary, with nontrivial, terminal-pair, and terminal-set variants. Every source–sink cut meets every directed source–sink path, while every inclusion-minimal arc set meeting all such paths is a source–sink cut.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The maximum is taken over all collections of directed cuts. The notation k∈Z_+ is retained without choosing a convention for whether zero is included.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Directed Graph and Arc Conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a loopless simple-digraph convention while recording standard reductions for undirected and parallel arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A directed graph is \(\mathcal G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\), where \(1\le |\mathcal N|=N<\infty\) and \(0\le |\mathcal A|=A<\infty\), and every arc is an ordered pair \((i,j)\) of distinct nodes. Arc \((i,j)\) starts at \(i\), ends at \(j\), is outgoing from \(i\), incoming to \(j\), and incident to both endpoints; the degree of a node is the number of incident arcs. The graph is complete when \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\) for every ordered pair of distinct nodes. Antiparallel arcs \((i,j)\) and \((j,i)\) may both occur, but at most one arc has any given ordered endpoint pair. An undirected edge \(\{i,j\}\) may be represented by two oppositely directed arcs with identical attributes, while a parallel arc from \(i\) to \(j\) may be represented using a new node \(n\) and arcs \((i,n),(n,j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite directed graph has finitely many nodes and ordered arcs between distinct nodes. Arc orientation determines its start, end, incoming, and outgoing incidences; completeness means that every ordered pair of distinct nodes is an arc. Opposite-direction arcs are allowed, but the adopted convention excludes parallel arcs with identical orientation. Undirected edges and parallel arcs can be represented by standard directed-graph transformations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a finite loopless directed graph with the stated incidence, completeness, and multiplicity conventions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjacency-List Representation of a Directed Network
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines linked outgoing-adjacency lists, node entry pointers, optional arc attributes, and mate pointers for paired reverse arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node \(i\) of a directed network, an adjacency-list representation stores one singly linked cell for every outgoing arc \((i,j)\in A\). Each cell stores at least the head \(j\), may also store attributes such as \(c_{ij}\) and \(u_{ij}\), and contains a link to the next cell, with link value \(0\) at the end. An array \(\operatorname{first}(i)\) points to the first cell for node \(i\), with \(\operatorname{first}(i)=0\) exactly when its list is empty. If every represented arc \((i,j)\) has a represented reversal \((j,i)\), an optional mate field in each cell may point directly to the reversal's cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacency-list representation keeps one singly linked list per node, with one cell for each outgoing arc. A cell stores the head node, optionally the arc's cost and capacity, and a link to the next cell; a zero link terminates the list. An array points to each node's first cell, using zero for an empty list. When reverse arcs are also present, an optional mate pointer can directly connect each arc cell to the cell for its reversal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-unblocked arcs, admissible graph, and augmenting paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions used by the auction/sequential shortest path method for a flow-price pair satisfying epsilon-complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(x,p)$ satisfy $\epsilon$-CS. An original arc $(i,j)$ is $\epsilon^+$-unblocked when $p_i=p_j+a_{ij}+\epsilon$ and $x_{ij}<c_{ij}$; an original arc $(j,i)$ is $\epsilon^-$-unblocked toward $i\to j$ when $p_i=p_j-a_{ji}+\epsilon$ and $b_{ji}<x_{ji}$. The admissible graph contains precisely these corresponding forward and reverse directions. A path is $\epsilon$-unblocked when every forward arc is $\epsilon^+$-unblocked and every backward arc is $\epsilon^-$-unblocked. Such a path $P$ is augmenting if $g_{s(P)}>0$ and $g_{t(P)}<0$, and augmentation changes every path arc by the common amount $\delta=\min\{g_{s(P)},-g_{t(P)},\min_{(i,j)\in P^+}(c_{ij}-x_{ij}),\min_{(i,j)\in P^-}(x_{ij}-b_{ij})\}$. A contraction deletes the terminal node and terminal arc; an extension appends an incident arc and its other endpoint, with a single-node path permitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a flow-price pair satisfying epsilon-complementary slackness, admissible directions are nonsaturated tight forward arcs and above-lower-bound tight reverse arcs. An epsilon-unblocked path uses only such directions. It is augmenting when it joins a positive-surplus start to a negative-surplus terminal, and its augmentation amount is the minimum of the two endpoint surplus magnitudes and all forward and backward residual capacities. Paths may be contracted at their terminal end or extended by one incident arc, and may initially contain one node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G^*\text{ and the notions of }\epsilon\text{-unblocked and augmenting paths are defined as above, with augmentation increment }\delta.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc Attribute Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite collections of arc-indexed data used by network models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. An arc attribute system is a finite indexed family \(\mathcal A=(\alpha_j:A\to X_j)_{j\in J}\), where each codomain \(X_j\) specifies the admissible values of attribute \(j\). Equivalently, it is a map \(\alpha:A\to\prod_{j\in J}X_j\) with coordinates \(\alpha_j\). Typical coordinates include capacity, lower bound, cost, length, or label; parallel arcs remain distinct arguments and may carry different attribute vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc attribute system assigns each arc a finite tuple of values, such as capacities, costs, bounds, lengths, or labels.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A=(\alpha_j)_{j\in J}\) assigns the attribute vector \(\alpha(a)=(\alpha_j(a))_{j\in J}\) to every \(a\in A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced graph of a bounded feasible flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the directed graph in which augmenting paths are sought.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a capacity-feasible flow $x$ on a directed graph with lower bounds $b_{ij}$ and upper capacities $c_{ij}$, its reduced graph has the original node set and contains, for every original arc $(i,j)$, a forward arc $(i,j)$ when $x_{ij}<c_{ij}$ and a reverse arc $(j,i)$ when $b_{ij}<x_{ij}$. Thus both arcs occur when $b_{ij}<x_{ij}<c_{ij}$.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An auction-form residual push and node-price update for a capacitated minimum-cost flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a selected node \(i\) with positive surplus \(g_i\), scan for a forward residual arc \((i,j)\) satisfying \(x_{ij}<c_{ij}\) and \(p_i=a_{ij}+p_j+\epsilon\), or a backward residual arc \((j,i)\) satisfying \(x_{ji}>0\) and \(p_i=p_j-a_{ji}+\epsilon\). On a forward arc, set \(x_{ij}\leftarrow x_{ij}+\min\{g_i,c_{ij}-x_{ij}\}\); on a backward arc, set \(x_{ji}\leftarrow x_{ji}-\min\{g_i,x_{ji}\}\). If no eligible arc exists, set
\[
p_i\leftarrow\min\left\{\min_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A:\,x_{ij}<c_{ij}}(a_{ij}+p_j+\epsilon),\;\min_{(j,i)\in\mathcal A:\,b_{ji}<x_{ji}}(p_j-a_{ji}+\epsilon)\right\}
\]
and resume scanning. After a push, stop when \(g_i=0\) and the used arc remains residual; otherwise resume scanning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-surplus node, push flow along a forward or backward residual arc whose price relation is tight up to epsilon. Forward and backward pushes are limited respectively by residual capacity or current flow and by the node surplus. If no eligible arc exists, raise the node price to the minimum epsilon-adjusted reduced-cost threshold among incident residual arcs. This iteration is the epsilon-relaxation method.
assumptions_latex: i\text{ is the selected node and }g_i>0
b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\text{for each arc }(i,j)\in\mathcal A
a_{ij}\text{ is the cost of arc }(i,j),\qquad \epsilon>0
\text{The residual-incident-arc set in the price update is nonempty when the update is invoked.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration applies residual flow pushes and an }\epsilon\text{-adjusted node-price increase; it is the }\epsilon\text{-relaxation method.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit arc-capacity reoptimization by residual shortest paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of an optimal minimum-cost flow to increasing or decreasing one integral arc capacity by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ be an optimal minimum-cost flow and change the capacity $u_{pq}$ by one unit. For $u'_{pq}=u_{pq}+1$, if $c_{pq}^{\pi}\ge 0$, then $x^*$ remains optimal. If $c_{pq}^{\pi}<0$, increase $x_{pq}$ by one and augment one unit from $q$ to $p$ along a shortest path in $G(x^*)$; the resulting flow is optimal and the objective changes by $c_{pq}+d(q,p)$. For $u'_{pq}=u_{pq}-1$, if $x^*_{pq}<u_{pq}$, then $x^*$ remains feasible and optimal. If $x^*_{pq}=u_{pq}$, decrease $x_{pq}$ by one and augment one unit from $p$ to $q$ along a shortest residual path; the resulting flow is optimal and the objective changes by $-c_{pq}+d(p,q)$. In the latter case, absence of a directed $p$-$q$ residual path implies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After increasing an arc capacity by one, the old optimum remains optimal when the arc has nonnegative reduced cost; otherwise add one unit on the arc and return it along a shortest residual path. After decreasing capacity by one, the old optimum remains optimal if the arc was not saturated; if it was saturated, remove one unit and reroute it along a shortest residual path. Failure of the required path in the capacity-decrease case certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal minimum-cost flow}
c_{pq}^{\pi}\text{ is the reduced cost under optimal potentials }\pi
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u'_{pq}=u_{pq}+1:\ c_{pq}^{\pi}\ge0\Rightarrow x^*\text{ remains optimal},\ c_{pq}^{\pi}<0\Rightarrow\Delta z^*=c_{pq}+d(q,p);\quad u'_{pq}=u_{pq}-1:\ x^*_{pq}<u_{pq}\Rightarrow x^*\text{ remains optimal},\ x^*_{pq}=u_{pq}\Rightarrow\Delta z^*=-c_{pq}+d(p,q),\text{ with infeasibility if }p\not\leadsto q.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit arc-cost increase by zero-reduced-cost rerouting and potential update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reoptimization of an optimal minimum-cost flow when one integral arc cost increases by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x^*$ be an optimal minimum-cost flow with integral arc costs, and increase $c_{pq}$ by one. If the original reduced cost satisfies $c_{pq}^{\pi}<0$ or $c_{pq}^{\pi}>0$, the modified reduced cost remains respectively nonpositive or nonnegative, so $x^*$ preserves the reduced-cost optimality conditions. The only nontrivial case is $c_{pq}^{\pi}=0$ and $x^*_{pq}>0$. Set $x_{pq}=0$ and send at most $x^*_{pq}$ units from $p$ to $q$ using only zero-reduced-cost residual arcs; let the maximum value be $v^{\circ}$. If $v^{\circ}=x^*_{pq}$, the resulting flow is optimal and the optimal objective value is unchanged. If $v^{\circ}<x^*_{pq}$, let $[S,\bar S]$ be the resulting minimum cut with $p\in S$ and $q\in\bar S$, decrease every potential in $\bar S$ by one, and set $x_{pq}=x^*_{pq}-v^{\circ}$. The resulting feasible flow is optimal, and the modified optimal objective exceeds the original by $x^*_{pq}-v^{\circ}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an integral arc cost rises by one, the old optimum usually remains optimal. The exceptional case is a zero-reduced-cost arc carrying positive flow. Remove its flow and reroute as much as possible from its tail to its head using only zero-reduced-cost residual arcs. Complete rerouting gives an optimum with unchanged value. Otherwise, use the resulting cut to shift potentials on the sink side and restore the unrouted flow on the changed arc; this gives an optimum whose value rises by the unrouted amount.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is an optimal minimum-cost flow}
c_{pq}^{\pi}\text{ is the reduced cost before the change}
v^{\circ}\text{ is the maximum }p\text{-}q\text{ flow of value at most }x^*_{pq}\text{ using only zero-reduced-cost residual arcs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c_{pq}^{\pi}\ne0\Rightarrow x^*\text{ preserves optimality};\quad c_{pq}^{\pi}=0,\ x^*_{pq}>0:\ v^{\circ}=x^*_{pq}\Rightarrow z'^*=z^*,\quad v^{\circ}<x^*_{pq}\Rightarrow z'^*=z^*+x^*_{pq}-v^{\circ}\text{ after the cut-based potential update}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for finite digraphs, including loop conventions and distinctions among ordered cuts, boundary cuts, dicuts, and rooted cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A digraph $D=(V,A)$ has finite nonempty $V$ and arcs associated with ordered endpoint pairs $(u,v)$, with tail $u$ and head $v$; loops are excluded unless explicitly allowed. For $B\subseteq A$ and $W\subseteq V$, $V(B)$ is the set of arc endnodes and $A(W)$ contains arcs with both ends in $W$; deletion and contraction follow the undirected definitions. The underlying graph has edge $ij$ iff $(i,j)\in A$ or $(j,i)\in A$, and an undirected property of $D$ means that property holds for its underlying graph. Define $\delta^+(v)$ and $\delta^-(v)$ as arcs leaving and entering $v$, with outdegree, indegree, and degree their respective cardinalities. For $\varnothing
e W
e V$, $\delta^+(W)=\{(i,j)\in A:i\in W,j
otin W\}$, $\delta^-(W)=\delta^+(V\setminus W)$, and $\delta(W)=\delta^+(W)\cup\delta^-(W)$. For distinct $s,t$, an $(s,t)$-cut is $\delta^+(W)$ and an $[s,t]$-boundary cut is $\delta(W)$ for some $W$ with $s\in W,t
otin W$. A directed cut or dicut is $\delta^+(W)$ when $\delta^-(W)=\varnothing$. For $r\in V$, an $r$-rooted cut is $\delta^-(W)$ for some $\varnothing
e W\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite digraph has arcs with ordered tail and head endpoints, with loops allowed only when stated. The packet defines induced arc and endpoint sets, deletion and contraction, the underlying undirected graph, incoming and outgoing incidence and degrees, outgoing, incoming and total boundaries of a vertex set, ordered terminal cuts, two-way boundary cuts, dicuts with no entering arcs, and cuts separating a nonempty set from a designated root.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed graphs and basic directed-graph terminology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Allows parallel arcs and loops and defines the principal derived objects and vertex-arc terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph is D=(V,A), where V is finite and A is a family of ordered pairs of vertices; repetitions are parallel arcs with multiplicity, and pairs (v,v) are loops. D is simple if it has neither loops nor multiple arcs and loopless if it has no loops. Its underlying undirected graph is (V,\{\{u,v\}:(u,v)\in A\}), and D is then an orientation of that graph. For a=(u,v), u is the tail and v the head; \delta_D^{\rm in}(v) and \delta_D^{\rm out}(v) are the entering and leaving arc families, with degrees equal to their cardinalities. A vertex of indegree zero is a source and one of outdegree zero is a sink. The reverse digraph is D^{-1}=(V,\{(v,u):(u,v)\in A\}). A mixed graph is a triple (V,E,A) consisting of undirected and directed edges on V.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed graph has a finite vertex set and a family of ordered vertex pairs, so parallel arcs and loops may occur. The definition specifies simple and loopless digraphs, the underlying undirected graph and orientations, tails and heads, entering and leaving arcs and neighbors, indegrees and outdegrees, sources and sinks, arc and graph reversal, and mixed graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel-Arc Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc multiplicity with identical ordered endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph with endpoint map \((\tau,\eta):A\to V\times V\). Distinct arcs \(a,b\in A\) are parallel when \(\tau(a)=\tau(b)\) and \(\eta(a)=\eta(b)\). For \((u,v)\in V\times V\), the parallel class is \(A_{uv}=\{a\in A:\tau(a)=u,\ \eta(a)=v\}\), and its multiplicity is \(m_{uv}=|A_{uv}|\). The digraph has parallel-arc structure when \(m_{uv}\ge 2\) for some ordered pair \((u,v)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel arcs are distinct arcs having the same tail and the same head; their multiplicity is the size of the corresponding endpoint class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) and \(b\) are parallel exactly when \((\tau(a),\eta(a))=(\tau(b),\eta(b))\).

notation.meaning: arcs directed from u to v

knowledge_statements.title: Antiparallel-Arc Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oppositely oriented arcs joining the same two distinct vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. Arcs \(a,b\in A\) are antiparallel when their endpoints are reversed: \(\tau(a)=\eta(b)\), \(\eta(a)=\tau(b)\), and \(\tau(a)\ne\eta(a)\). Equivalently, for distinct vertices \(u,v\in V\), every arc in \(A_{uv}\) is antiparallel to every arc in \(A_{vu}\). The digraph has antiparallel-arc structure when both \(A_{uv}\) and \(A_{vu}\) are nonempty for some \(u\ne v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antiparallel arcs connect the same two distinct vertices in opposite directions; such structure exists when arcs occur in both directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) and \(b\) are antiparallel exactly when \((\tau(a),\eta(a))=(\eta(b),\tau(b))\) with distinct endpoints.

notation.meaning: arcs directed from u to v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States a subdivision convention used to prevent multiple ordered-arc copies in residual networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) belong to \(A\), then \(N(f)\) may contain multiple copies of an ordered arc. One may replace an arc \((u,v)\) of capacity \(b(u,v)\) by \((u,w)\) and \((w,v)\), each of capacity \(b(u,v)\), where \(w\) is a new vertex. After applying such subdivisions as needed, the subsequent analysis assumes that \(N(f)\) has no multiple arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antiparallel original arcs can produce multiple copies in a residual network. Subdividing an arc through a new vertex, while retaining its capacity on both replacement arcs, permits the analysis to assume that residual networks have no multiple arcs.

knowledge_statements.title: Source Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural sources in a directed graph, distinguished from designated flow sources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A vertex \(v\in V\) is a source vertex when no arc enters it, equivalently when \(\delta^-(v)=\varnothing\) or its indegree satisfies \(d^-(v)=0\). This structural definition does not require \(v\) to have a positive outdegree. A vertex designated to supply flow may also be called a source in flow models even when incoming arcs exist; that model-specific usage is separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structural source has indegree zero. A designated flow source is a separate modeling role and need not have indegree zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is a structural source exactly when \(\delta^-(v)=\varnothing\), equivalently \(d^-(v)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Designated endpoint vertices in a directed network model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A terminal system is a specified subset \(T\subseteq V\); each \(v\in T\) is a terminal vertex. Terminal status is model data rather than an intrinsic degree property. When endpoints have distinct roles, one may specify disjoint subsets \(T^+,T^-\subseteq V\) of source and sink terminals and set \(T=T^+\cup T^-\). Depending on the model, paths, demands, or nonzero flow balances are required to begin or end at terminals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminal is a vertex explicitly designated as an allowed endpoint; terminal status is model data and imposes no degree condition by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(T\subseteq V\) is specified as part of the model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\) is a terminal vertex exactly when \(v\in T\).

knowledge_statements.title: Root Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Out-roots defined by directed reachability from one distinguished vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a directed multigraph. A vertex \(r\in V\) is an out-root, or root under the outward convention, when every vertex \(v\in V\) is reachable from \(r\) by a directed path. Equivalently, \(D\) contains a spanning out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) when \(V\) is finite. Under the dual inward convention, a root is reachable from every vertex; the chosen convention must therefore be stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the outward convention, a root reaches every vertex by a directed path; the inward convention reverses all reachability directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\) is an out-root exactly when for every \(v\in V\) there exists a directed path from \(r\) to \(v\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The outward-reachability definition and finite spanning-out-arborescence equivalence are plausible, but no citation is supplied. An authoritative locator is required, particularly because inward and outward root conventions coexist.

knowledge_statements.title: Source–Sink Flow Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite single-commodity feasible flows with one designated source and one designated sink, including arc lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed multigraph, let distinct vertices \(s,t\in V\) be designated, and let arc bounds satisfy \(0\le \ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). A feasible source–sink flow of value \(F\ge 0\) is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) and \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=\begin{cases}F,&v=s,\\-F,&v=t,\\0,&v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}.\end{cases}\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible source–sink flow on a finite directed network obeys every arc bound, conserves flow at all vertices other than the designated source and sink, and has equal nonnegative source excess and sink deficit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible with value \(F\ge 0\) exactly when it satisfies the arc bounds and has divergence \(F\) at \(s\), \(-F\) at \(t\), and \(0\) at every other vertex.

notation.meaning: lower and upper flow bounds on arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition using paths that are vertex-disjoint except at their common terminal node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph with at least $k+1$ vertices and no parallel edges. For $Z\subseteq V$ and $v\in V$, let $\kappa^+(Z,v)$ be the maximum number of directed paths from $Z$ to $v$ that are mutually vertex-disjoint except for their common terminal vertex $v$. A set $Z\subseteq V$ is a $k$-source if
\[
\kappa^+(Z,v)\ge k\qquad\text{for every }v\in V\setminus Z.
\]
In particular, $V$ is a $k$-source.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a digraph with at least k+1 vertices and no parallel edges, a subset Z is a k-source when every vertex outside Z can be reached from Z by at least k directed paths that are vertex-disjoint except at their common terminal vertex. The full vertex set is always a k-source.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph with no parallel edges}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z\text{ is a }k\text{-source}\iff \kappa^+(Z,v)\ge k\text{ for every }v\in V\setminus Z;\quad V\text{ is a }k\text{-source}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The flow-change phase following successful residual labeling of the sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta=\xi(t)\). Starting at \(t\), follow predecessor labels back to \(s\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node–arc definition of a single-commodity static flow, its capacity constraints, conservation equations, and value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=[N;\alpha]\) have a capacity function \(c:\alpha\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\), optionally with infinite capacities, and let \(s,t\in N\) be distinguished nodes. A static flow of value \(v\) from \(s\) to \(t\) is a function \(f:\alpha\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}\) satisfying \[\sum_{y:(x,y)\in\alpha}f(x,y)-\sum_{y:(y,x)\in\alpha}f(y,x)=\begin{cases}v,&x=s,\\0,&x\notin\{s,t\},\\-v,&x=t,\end{cases}\] and \(f(x,y)\le c(x,y)\) for every \((x,y)\in\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated static source–sink flow is a nonnegative arc function bounded by arc capacities. Its net outflow is its value at the source, the negative of that value at the sink, and zero at every intermediate node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a static }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of value }v\iff 0\le f(a)\le c(a)\text{ for all }a\in\alpha\text{ and the stated node balances hold.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-flow formulation with directional capacities, intermediate-node conservation, and throughput maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a directed network have source $0$, sink $n$, directional arc capacities $\alpha_{ij}\ge 0$, and arc flows $x_{ij}$. Feasibility requires $0\le x_{ij}\le\alpha_{ij}$ on every network arc and $\sum_i x_{ik}-\sum_j x_{kj}=0$ for $k=1,\ldots,n-1$. Define the flow value $F$ by $F+\sum_i x_{i0}-\sum_jx_{0j}=0$. Conservation then gives $\sum_i x_{in}-\sum_jx_{nj}=F$. The maximum-flow problem maximizes $F$ subject to these constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated source–sink maximum-flow problem chooses nonnegative directional arc flows within capacity, conserves flow at every intermediate node, and maximizes the net flow leaving the source, which equals the net flow entering the sink.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max F\quad\text{subject to}\quad F+\sum_i x_{i0}-\sum_jx_{0j}=0,\qquad \sum_i x_{in}-\sum_jx_{nj}=F

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual labeling routine for an augmenting path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The search phase of the Ford–Fulkerson labeling method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the source label with bottleneck value \(\xi(s)=\infty\). Repeatedly scan a labeled node \(x\): label each unlabeled \(y\) with predecessor sign \(+\) when \(f(x,y)<c(x,y)\), setting \(\xi(y)=\min\{\xi(x),c(x,y)-f(x,y)\}\); then label each still-unlabeled \(y\) with predecessor sign \(-\) when \(f(y,x)>0\), setting \(\xi(y)=\min\{\xi(x),f(y,x)\}\). Continue until \(t\) is labeled or no further label is possible. In the first case invoke flow augmentation; in the second terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Label the source and scan labeled vertices through forward arcs having unused capacity and backward arcs carrying positive flow. Each new label records its predecessor, direction, and the minimum residual amount along the discovered route. Stop when the sink is reached, triggering augmentation, or when no new vertex can be labeled, triggering termination.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible flow from source \(s\) to sink \(t\) in a network with capacities \(c\).
Initially \(s\) is labeled and unscanned, while every other node is unlabeled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\text{ is labeled with an augmenting predecessor chain, or no further residual-reachable node exists.}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Optimality for the Parameterized Flow Objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source notation for the algorithmically generated flows and node labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The flows $r_p$ and $r_{p+1}$ maximize $p\,v(r)-\sum_{(x,y)}a(x,y)r(x,y)$ over all source-to-sink flows. The node integers $\tau_p$ and arc integers $\gamma_p(x,y)=\max\{0,\tau_p(y)-\tau_p(x)-a(x,y)\}$ solve the dual program, and $$p v_p-\sum_{(x,y)}a(x,y)r_p(x,y)=p v_{p+1}-\sum_{(x,y)}a(x,y)r_{p+1}(x,y)=\sum_{(x,y)}c(x,y)\gamma_p(x,y).$$

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bottleneck-removal algorithm for a blocking flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a blocking flow by repeatedly augmenting through a minimum-capacity node on the maintained source–sink chain and deleting internal bottlenecks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting at the source, follow the successor pointers \(A\) to the sink and choose a node \(w\) of minimum \(C(w)\) on this chain. If \(C(w)>0\), set \(d=C(w)\), dispatch \(d\) units from \(w\) toward the sink using repeated \(\operatorname{PUSHRIGHT}\) calls with the maintained surpluses, and dispatch \(d\) units from the source toward \(w\) using repeated \(\operatorname{PUSHLEFT}\) calls. If \(w\) is the source or sink, stop; otherwise call \(\operatorname{REMOVE}(w)\) and repeat. Upon termination, the accumulated core flow is blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly find a minimum-capacity bottleneck on the current source–sink chain, send its capacity through the chain in both directions from that bottleneck, and remove it if it is internal. Stop when the selected bottleneck is a terminal; the accumulated core flow is blocking.
assumptions_latex: A layered source--sink core and the quantities \(A,B,C,S\) are maintained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm terminates with a blocking feasible flow in the core.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated directed source–sink flow with prescribed positive integer throughput.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed graph with source $1$, sink $N$, no arcs entering $1$, and no arcs leaving $N$. Given $s\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ and capacities $c_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$, the fixed-flow problem is to find $x$ satisfying
\[\sum_{j:(i,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{ij}-\sum_{j:(j,i)\in\mathcal A}x_{ji}=0\quad\forall i\in\mathcal N\setminus\{1,N\},\]
\[\sum_{j:(1,j)\in\mathcal A}x_{1j}=\sum_{j:(j,N)\in\mathcal A}x_{jN}=s,\]
and
\[0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}\quad\forall(i,j)\in\mathcal A.\]
Here $s$ is prescribed, whereas in the maximum-flow problem it is maximized. If $s$ equals the maximum feasible flow value, the two problems coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-flow problem asks for a prescribed positive integer amount s to be sent from a designated source to a designated sink while respecting capacities and conserving flow at all other nodes. It coincides with maximum flow when s is the maximum feasible throughput.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is directed, with no arcs entering source }1\text{ and no arcs leaving sink }N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The feasible vectors are precisely capacity-bounded source–sink flows of prescribed value }s;\text{ at the maximum feasible }s\text{ the fixed-flow and max-flow problems coincide.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Source–Sink Networks, Flows, Values, and Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for finite directed source–sink networks with nonnegative real arc capacities; lower arc bounds are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A network is a quadruple $(D,c,s,t)$, where $D=(V,E)$ is a finite digraph, $s,t\in V$ are distinguished source and sink vertices, and $c:E	o\mathbb R_+$ assigns arc capacities. A flow is a function $f:E	o\mathbb R_+$ satisfying $\sum_u f(u,v)=\sum_w f(v,w)$ for every $v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}$ and $f(u,v)\le c(u,v)$ for every $(u,v)\in E$. Its value is $\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_u f(s,u)-\sum_u f(u,s)=\sum_u f(u,t)-\sum_u f(t,u)$. For $A\subseteq V$ with $s\in A$ and $t
otin A$, the associated $s$-$t$ cut is $
abla^+(A)=\{(u,v)\in E:u\in A,
v
otin A\}$ and has capacity $\operatorname{cap}(A)=\sum_{u\in A,\,v
otin A}c(u,v)$. Since $D$ is finite, a minimum-capacity $s$-$t$ cut exists. Extending $f$ and $c$ by zero on vertex pairs having no arc in either direction is an optional convention. The usual augmenting-flow iteration is guaranteed to terminate after finitely many iterations under integral capacities, but not for arbitrary real capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite source–sink network consists of a digraph, a source, a sink, and nonnegative real arc capacities. A flow is nonnegative, respects capacities, and is conserved at every nonterminal vertex. Its value is the net flow leaving the source, equivalently the net flow entering the sink. A source-side vertex set determines a directed source–sink cut whose capacity is the sum of capacities leaving the set. A minimum cut exists because the graph has finitely many cuts. Values may optionally be extended by zero to vertex pairs with no arc in either direction. Lower arc bounds are not included, and finite termination of the usual augmentation procedure is guaranteed for integral capacities but not for arbitrary real capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is feasible}\iff\left[\forall v\in V\setminus\{s,t\},\ \sum_u f(u,v)=\sum_w f(v,w)\right]\land\left[\forall (u,v)\in E,\ f(u,v)\le c(u,v)\right],\quad \min_{A:\,s\in A,\,t\notin A}\operatorname{cap}(A)\text{ exists}.
