knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Ratio Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-cycle objective with a strictly positive denominator weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) carry numerator weights \(a:E\to\mathbb R\) and denominator weights \(b:E\to\mathbb R_{>0}\). For every nonempty directed cycle \(C\), define \[\rho(C)=\frac{\sum_{e\in C}a(e)}{\sum_{e\in C}b(e)}.\] The minimum-ratio-cycle value is \[\rho^*=\min\{\rho(C):C\text{ is a directed cycle of }G\}.\] A cycle attaining \(\rho^*\) is a minimum-ratio cycle. Strict positivity of \(b(e)\) makes every cycle denominator positive and the ratio well-defined. If no directed cycle exists, the problem is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-ratio cycle minimizes the sum of numerator weights divided by the positive sum of denominator weights over directed cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cycle \(C^*\) is minimum-ratio exactly when \(\rho(C^*)=\rho^*\).

notation.meaning: positive denominator weight of arc e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-denominator minimum-ratio-cycle definition is mathematically precise and fits the container, but no authoritative source or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum cost-to-time ratio cycle and parametric test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the cycle-ratio objective and the transformed-length tests for a trial ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a directed graph with integral arc costs \(c_{ij}\) and travel times \(\tau_{ij}\ge 0\), and suppose \(\tau(W)=\sum_{(i,j)\in W}\tau_{ij}>0\) for every directed cycle \(W\). Then
\[\mu^*=\min_{W}\frac{c(W)}{\tau(W)},\qquad c(W)=\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}.\]
For a trial value \(\mu\), set \(l_{ij}=c_{ij}-\mu\tau_{ij}\). If some directed cycle has negative length, then \(\mu>\mu^*\). If no directed cycle has negative length and some cycle \(W^*\) has zero length, then \(\mu=\mu^*\) and \(W^*\) is optimal. If every directed cycle has positive length, then \(\mu<\mu^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum cost-to-time ratio cycle minimizes total cost divided by positive total travel time. Under lengths equal to cost minus a trial ratio times travel time, a negative cycle shows that the trial ratio is too high; a zero cycle in the absence of negative cycles certifies optimality; and strictly positive lengths for every cycle show that the trial ratio is too low.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu^*=\min_W\frac{c(W)}{\tau(W)},\quad l(W)<0\Rightarrow\mu>\mu^*,\quad \bigl(l(W)\ge0\ \forall W\text{ and }l(W^*)=0\bigr)\Rightarrow\mu=\mu^*,\quad l(W)>0\ \forall W\Rightarrow\mu<\mu^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum mean cycle and exact-length-walk dynamic program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the specialization and its dynamic-programming quantities and running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Setting \(\tau_{ij}=1\) for every arc reduces the minimum-ratio-cycle objective to \[\mu^*=\min_W\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}}{|W|}.\] In a strongly connected directed network, fix a node \(s\), and let \(d^k(j)\) be the minimum cost of an \(s\)-to-\(j\) directed walk containing exactly \(k\) arcs. These values satisfy \[d^k(j)=\min_{(i,j)\in A}\{d^{k-1}(i)+c_{ij}\}.\] Computing all \(d^k(j)\) for \(k=1,\ldots,n\) takes \(O(nm)\) time. Strong connectivity may be enforced by sufficiently expensive added arcs, which cannot enter a minimum mean cycle unless the original network is acyclic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary search for an integral minimum-ratio cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines negative-cycle decisions with separation between distinct integral cycle ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \([\underline\mu,\overline\mu]\) contain \(\mu^*\). At each iteration test the midpoint \(\mu^\circ=(\underline\mu+\overline\mu)/2\) using lengths \(c_{ij}-\mu^\circ\tau_{ij}\). If a negative cycle exists, set \(\overline\mu=\mu^\circ\); otherwise set \(\underline\mu=\mu^\circ\). For integral data, if \(\tau_0=\max_{(i,j)\in A}\tau_{ij}\), the extract asserts that two distinct cycle ratios differ by at least \(1/\tau_0^2\). Starting from \([-C,C]\), where \(C=\max_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}\), it therefore gives \(O(\log(\tau_0C))\) iterations before the interval contains at most one cycle ratio; a zero-length cycle for lengths \(c_{ij}-\overline\mu\tau_{ij}\) is then optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary search maintains an interval containing the optimal cycle ratio and uses negative-cycle detection to choose the appropriate half. Under the extract's integral-data separation bound, the interval isolates a unique cycle ratio after logarithmically many iterations, after which a zero-length cycle is optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The interval is halved per iteration and, under the stated separation claim, isolates }\mu^*\text{ in }O(\log(\tau_0C))\text{ iterations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential search for a minimum-ratio cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successively tightens an upper bound using negative-cycle witnesses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Start from a known upper bound \(\mu^0\ge\mu^*\). At iteration \(r\), use arc lengths \(c_{ij}-\mu^r\tau_{ij}\). If a zero-length cycle \(W\) is found and there is no negative cycle, return \(W\) as a minimum-ratio cycle. If a negative cycle \(W\) is found, set \[\mu^{r+1}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in W}c_{ij}}{\sum_{(i,j)\in W}\tau_{ij}}.\] Then \(\mu^r>\mu^{r+1}\ge\mu^*\); repetition produces a strictly decreasing sequence of cycle ratios terminating at \(\mu^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Beginning with an upper bound on the optimal ratio, repeatedly detect a negative cycle under cost-minus-ratio-times-time lengths and replace the bound by that cycle's ratio. A zero-length cycle certifies termination, while every negative-cycle update strictly decreases the upper bound without passing below the optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu^0>\mu^1>\cdots>\mu^k=\mu^*,\qquad \mu^{r+1}=\frac{c(W_r)}{\tau(W_r)}\ge\mu^*.

knowledge_statements.title: Bottleneck Shortest Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax path objective on a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(s,t\in V\). The bottleneck value of an \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) is \(b(P)=\max_{e\in P}w(e)\). A bottleneck shortest path is any path \(P^*\) satisfying \[b(P^*)=\min\{b(P):P\text{ is an }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}.\] Equivalently, its value is the least threshold \(\lambda\) for which \(t\) is reachable from \(s\) in the subgraph \((V,\{e\in E:w(e)\leq\lambda\})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bottleneck shortest path minimizes its largest edge weight; its value is the smallest edge threshold making the target reachable.
assumptions_latex: At least one directed \(s\)-\(t\) path exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(P^*)=\min_{P:s\leadsto t}\max_{e\in P}w(e)\).

notation.meaning: maximum edge weight on path P

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dreyfus recurrence and complexity for M shortest walks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-origin ranked-walk computation with repeated vertices permitted and deterministic ordering of equal-length walks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let paths be walks that may repeat vertices, including the origin, and distinguish two walks by their vertex sequences; order equal-length walks lexicographically. Let $u_j^{[m]}$ be the length of the $m$th ranked walk from origin $1$ to vertex $j$, and let $\mu(k,j,m)$ count, among the first $m$ such walks to $j$, those whose final arc is $(k,j)$, with $\mu(k,j,0)=0$. Then
\[
u_j^{[m+1]}=\min_k\left\{u_k^{[\mu(k,j,m)+1]}+a_{kj}\right\},\qquad u_1^{[1]}=0.
\]
After the ordinary shortest walks are computed, processing vertices by the number of arcs in their first shortest walks makes the recurrence explicit. With a heap-based implementation, the first $M$ ranked walks from the origin to every vertex require $O(Mn\log n)$ additional time and $Mn+m'$ words of storage, where $m'$ is the number of arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allow walks to repeat vertices and distinguish them by their vertex sequences, breaking equal-length ties lexicographically. For each destination, the next ranked walk is obtained by choosing a final incoming arc and using the next not-yet-consumed ranked walk to its tail. Processing vertices in order of the arc count of their first shortest walks makes these dependencies explicit. After the initial shortest-path computation, the first M ranked walks to all vertices can be computed in O(M n log n) additional time using M n plus the number of arcs words of storage.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,A)\text{ is a directed network with }|V|=n\text{ and }|A|=m'.
\text{Walks are distinguished by vertex sequence, and equal lengths are ordered lexicographically.}
u_j^{[m]}\text{ and the required ranked walks are well-defined for }1\le m\le M.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u_j^{[m+1]}=\min_k\{u_k^{[\mu(k,j,m)+1]}+a_{kj}\},\quad\text{with additional time }O(Mn\log n)\text{ and storage }Mn+m'.

children.title: Dense-Graph Complexity
children.top_down_role: Shortest-path performance in high-density graph representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source Dijkstra complexity with an array-based minimum selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and nonnegative edge lengths. Dijkstra's algorithm implemented with an unsorted array performs at most \(n\) minimum-label scans costing \(O(n)\) each and \(O(m)\) total relaxations. Its running time is therefore \(O(n^2+m)\), which is \(O(n^2)\) when \(m=\Theta(n^2)\); its storage requirement is \(O(n+m)\) under adjacency-list storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Array-based Dijkstra runs in quadratic time on dense nonnegatively weighted graphs, with linear storage in the graph representation.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic, comparison, and adjacency-list access take unit time.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Graph Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heap-based single-source Dijkstra bounds for sparse graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and nonnegative edge lengths. With adjacency lists and a binary heap, Dijkstra's algorithm runs in \(O((n+m)\log n)\) time. With a Fibonacci heap, its amortized running time is \(O(m+n\log n)\). Thus, when \(m=O(n)\), these bounds become respectively \(O(n\log n)\) and \(O(n\log n)\), using \(O(n+m)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heap implementations make Dijkstra near-linear, up to logarithmic factors, on sparse nonnegatively weighted graphs.
assumptions_latex: The graph is stored by adjacency lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{binary}}=O((n+m)\log n)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{Fibonacci}}=O(m+n\log n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Structure Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Priority-queue choice controls Dijkstra's asymptotic running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Dijkstra's algorithm on a graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges of nonnegative length, the priority-queue implementation changes the bound: an unsorted array gives \(O(n^2+m)\), a binary heap gives \(O((n+m)\log n)\), and a Fibonacci heap gives amortized \(O(m+n\log n)\). Consequently, arrays are asymptotically competitive on dense graphs, whereas heaps expose the advantage of sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dijkstra's complexity changes from quadratic array scans to heap-sensitive bounds, so graph density determines the preferable priority queue.
assumptions_latex: The same adjacency-list relaxation scheme is used in all implementations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{array}}=O(n^2+m)\), \(T_{\mathrm{binary}}=O((n+m)\log n)\), and \(T_{\mathrm{Fibonacci}}=O(m+n\log n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Magnitude Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial dependence in bounded-integer shortest-path implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose all edge lengths are integers in \(\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\). A bucket implementation of Dijkstra's algorithm may have running time \(O(m+nC)\). This is polynomial in the numeric value \(C\) but not necessarily in its binary encoding length \(\lceil\log_2(C+1)\rceil\). Thus the bound is pseudo-polynomial: replacing \(C\) by \(2^kC\) can increase the running-time bound exponentially in the additional \(k\) input bits, although \(n\) and \(m\) are unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound polynomial in the largest integer weight can be exponential in that weight's bit length and is therefore only pseudo-polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(O(m+nC)\) is not generally polynomial in \(n+m+\log(C+1)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-model definition of weak polynomiality for numeric optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instances with combinatorial dimensions \(n,m\) and binary-encoded numerical data of total bit length \(L\), an algorithm is weakly polynomial when its running time is bounded by a polynomial in \(n,m,L\), but no bound polynomial solely in \(n,m\) is asserted for its arithmetic-operation count. Hence dependence polynomial in \(\log(C+1)\), where \(C\) bounds the data magnitudes, is compatible with weak polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly polynomial algorithm is polynomial in total input length but may depend on the bit lengths of numerical data.
assumptions_latex: Numerical input is encoded in binary.
Elementary bit operations are charged in the computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\leq\operatorname{poly}(n,m,L)\), possibly with essential dependence on \(L\).

children.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic-model definition of strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An algorithm for a numerically specified combinatorial problem is strongly polynomial if the number of arithmetic and comparison operations is bounded by a polynomial in the combinatorial dimensions \(n,m\), independently of the numerical values and their encoding lengths, and every intermediate number has encoding length bounded polynomially in the input length. Under these conditions, the algorithm also has polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strongly polynomial algorithm uses polynomially many arithmetic operations independent of numeric magnitudes and keeps all intermediate numbers polynomially encoded.
assumptions_latex: Input numbers are rational or integral and finitely encoded.
Arithmetic and comparisons are the primitive operations counted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{ops}}\leq\operatorname{poly}(n,m)\), independently of numerical magnitudes.

children.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary separating combinatorial input dependence from magnitude-sensitive performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Numeric-Dependence Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating pseudo-polynomial, weakly polynomial, and strongly polynomial running-time guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\geq 1\) bound the absolute values of binary-encoded numerical data. A running-time bound polynomial in \(C\) but not polynomial in the input encoding length is pseudo-polynomial. A bound polynomial in the full input encoding length may depend polynomially on \(\log(C+1)\) and is compatible with weak polynomiality. Strong polynomiality additionally requires the number of arithmetic and comparison operations to be bounded by a polynomial in the combinatorial dimensions alone, independently of \(C\) and its encoding length, with polynomially bounded intermediate encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial dependence on numeric magnitudes may be only pseudo-polynomial; polynomial dependence on encoding length is compatible with weak polynomiality; strong polynomiality requires a magnitude-independent operation bound and controlled intermediate encodings.
assumptions_latex: Numerical values are encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forms \(\operatorname{poly}(C)\), \(\operatorname{poly}(\log(C+1))\), and magnitude-independent arithmetic-operation bounds distinguish pseudo-polynomial, weakly polynomial, and strongly polynomial guarantees subject to their respective definitions.

children.title: Negative-Cycle Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Shortest-walk pathologies caused by reachable negative cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness criterion for minimum-weight walks between two vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with real edge weights and vertices \(s,t\). The infimum of the weights of directed \(s\)-\(t\) walks equals \(-\infty\) if and only if some negative-weight directed cycle is reachable from \(s\) and can itself reach \(t\). If no such cycle lies on the \(s\)-\(t\) corridor and an \(s\)-\(t\) walk exists, a minimum-weight walk exists and contains no repeated cycle of negative weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shortest-walk value is unbounded below exactly when an accessible negative cycle can still reach the target.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights are real and walk weight is additive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{W:s\leadsto t}w(W)=-\infty\) exactly when a negative cycle lies on an \(s\)-\(t\) walk.

notation.meaning: sum of edge weights along walk W

knowledge_statements.title: Simple-Path Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: NP-completeness caused by imposing vertex simplicity in the presence of negative edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the decision problem whose input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), vertices \(s,t\in V\), integer edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{Z}\), and an integer threshold \(B\): determine whether there is a simple directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\) with \(w(P)\leq B\). This problem is NP-complete even when \(w(e)=-1\) for every \(e\in E\). In that case \(w(P)=-|P|\), so the threshold condition can encode the existence of a directed Hamiltonian \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring a shortest path to be simple makes the decision problem NP-complete with unrestricted negative weights; weights of minus one encode a longest-simple-path threshold.
assumptions_latex: The weights and \(B\) are binary-encoded integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The decision problem \(\exists P\text{ simple directed from }s\text{ to }t:w(P)\leq B\) is NP-complete, even when \(w(e)=-1\) for every \(e\in E\).

children.title: Walk–Path Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Complexity separation between unrestricted walks and simple paths under negative lengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Walk–Path Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between tractable shortest walks and hard shortest simple paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with real edge weights, let \(s,t\in V\), and suppose an \(s\)-\(t\) walk exists. If no negative-weight directed cycle is reachable from \(s\) and able to reach \(t\), deleting repeated nonnegative-weight closed subwalks from a minimum-weight \(s\)-\(t\) walk yields a simple \(s\)-\(t\) path of no greater weight; hence the walk and simple-path optima coincide. If such a negative cycle exists, the walk infimum is \(-\infty\), whereas the simple-path optimum is finite; with unrestricted negative integer weights, computing the latter is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible source-target pair, shortest walks and shortest simple paths coincide when no relevant negative cycle exists. With such a cycle, walks are unbounded below while the finite simple-path problem is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\), and at least one directed \(s\)-\(t\) walk exists.
Walk weight is the sum of real edge weights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a relevant negative cycle, the walk and simple-path optima are equal; with one, the walk infimum is \(-\infty\) while the simple-path optimum remains finite and is NP-hard to compute for unrestricted negative integer weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bellman–Ford variant with arbitrary starting node, witness walks, and an O(nm) bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a digraph $D=(V,A)$ with $n=|V|$, $m=|A|$, and $c:A\to\mathbb R$, initialize $\pi_c^{(0)}(v)=0$ and, for $i=0,\ldots,n-1$, set
\[\pi_c^{(i+1)}(v)=\min\!\left\{\pi_c^{(i)}(v),\min_{uv\in A}\bigl(\pi_c^{(i)}(u)+c(uv)\bigr)\right\}.\]
Maintain a witness walk $W_c^{(i)}(v)$ by retaining the previous walk or appending the minimizing edge. Then $\pi_c^{(i)}(v)$ is the minimum cost of a walk ending at $v$ with at most $i$ edges, and $W_c^{(i)}(v)$ realizes it. After $n$ rounds the method yields a feasible potential when $c$ is conservative and otherwise a negative-circuit witness, in $O(nm)$ time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize every node label to zero and repeatedly relax every edge for n rounds, retaining a walk attaining each label. After round i, each label is the cheapest cost of a walk ending at that node and using at most i edges. The procedure produces either a feasible potential or a negative circuit and runs in O(nm) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi_c^{(i)}(v)=\min\{c(W):W\text{ ends at }v,\ |E(W)|\le i\};\qquad T(n,m)=O(nm),\text{ with output a feasible potential or a negative circuit.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes shortest-walk behavior, flow-formulation unboundedness, and simple-path complexity when negative directed cycles occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a directed network contains no negative-length directed cycle, cycles can be removed from a shortest directed walk without increasing its length, so a shortest walk can be chosen to be a path. If the network contains a negative directed cycle, the referenced flow linear-programming formulation is unbounded because arbitrarily much flow can be sent around that cycle. Requiring walks not to revisit nodes produces the simple shortest-path variant, which in this regime is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a negative directed cycle, some shortest walk can be made into a path by deleting cycles. A negative cycle makes the referenced flow formulation unbounded. If repeated nodes are prohibited, the resulting simple shortest-path problem in the negative-cycle regime is NP-complete.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Balanced k-way decomposition of an integer circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The componentwise floor-ceiling bounds hold for every circulation summand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A) be a digraph, let k\in\mathbb{Z}_+ with k\ge1, and let f:A\to\mathbb{Z} be a circulation. Then f=f_1+\cdots+f_k, where each f_i is an integer circulation satisfying \left\lfloor f/k\right\rfloor\le f_i\le\left\lceil f/k\right\rceil componentwise on A.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any integer circulation can be split into k integer circulations, each obtained by componentwise rounding the average f/k up or down.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathbb{Z}^A:\ f=\sum_{i=1}^k f_i,\quad f_i\text{ is a circulation},\quad \left\lfloor\frac{f}{k}\right\rfloor\le f_i\le\left\lceil\frac{f}{k}\right\rceil\ \forall i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Circulations and their nonnegative circuit decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a circulation and states the accompanying decomposition consequences under nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a digraph D=(V,A), a function f:A\to\mathbb{R} is a circulation if f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v)) for every v\in V. Every nonnegative circulation is a nonnegative linear combination of incidence vectors of directed circuits. Every nonnegative integer circulation is a sum of incidence vectors of directed circuits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circulation is an arc function with equal total inflow and outflow at every vertex. Every nonnegative circulation decomposes into directed circuits, and every nonnegative integer circulation is a sum of directed-circuit incidence vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a circulation}\iff (\forall v\in V)\ f(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=f(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(v));\quad f\ge0\implies f\in\operatorname{cone}\{\chi^C:C\text{ is a directed circuit}\};\quad f\in\mathbb{Z}_+^A\implies f\text{ is a sum of directed-circuit incidence vectors}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduction of bounded-circulation feasibility to maximum flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive reduction for rational two-sided arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a digraph \(D=(V,A)\) and \(d,c:A\to\mathbb Q\) with \(d\le c\), set \(c'(e)=c(e)-d(e)\) for each \(e\in A\). Add vertices \(s,t\); for each \(v\) with \(\operatorname{excess}_d(v)>0\), add \((s,v)\) with capacity \(\operatorname{excess}_d(v)\), and for each \(v\) with \(\operatorname{excess}_d(v)<0\), add \((v,t)\) with capacity \(-\operatorname{excess}_d(v)\). Then \(D\) has a circulation \(f\) satisfying \(d\le f\le c\) if and only if the extended network has an \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f'\le c'\) of value \(\sum_{v:\operatorname{excess}_d(v)>0}\operatorname{excess}_d(v)\). Recover the circulation by setting \(f(e)=f'(e)+d(e)\) for every \(e\in A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shift each original arc by its lower bound and connect a supersource and supersink to vertices with positive and negative lower-bound excess. Feasibility is equivalent to routing all positive excess, after which adding back the lower bounds recovers the circulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists f\text{ circulation}:d\le f\le c\iff\exists f'\text{ an }s\text{-}t\text{ flow}:f'\le c',\ |f'|=\sum_{v:\operatorname{excess}_d(v)>0}\operatorname{excess}_d(v),\quad f|_A=f'|_A+d.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the sparsity, endpoint, integral-coefficient, and construction-time guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D=(V,A) be a digraph and f:A\to\mathbb{R}_+. Then f=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\chi^{P_i}, where r\le |A|, \lambda_i\ge 0, and each P_i is a directed path or directed circuit. Each path begins at a vertex v with \operatorname{excess}_f(v)<0 and ends at a vertex w with \operatorname{excess}_f(w)>0. If f is integer-valued, the coefficients \lambda_i may be chosen integral. Such a decomposition can be found in O(nm) time, where n=|V| and m=|A|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonnegative arc function is a nonnegative combination of at most |A| directed paths and circuits. The paths go from negative-excess vertices to positive-excess vertices. Integer arc functions admit integer coefficients, and the decomposition can be found in O(nm) time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\sum_{i=1}^r\lambda_i\chi^{P_i},\quad r\le |A|,\quad \lambda_i\ge0,\quad \text{with the stated endpoint, integrality, and }O(nm)\text{ guarantees}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here l(U,V) and c(U,V) denote total lower bounds and capacities on arcs directed from U to V.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let every arc (x,y) have bounds 0\le l(x,y)\le c(x,y). A circulation f satisfying f(x,N)-f(N,x)=0 for every x\in N and l(x,y)\le f(x,y)\le c(x,y) for every arc exists if and only if c(X,\bar X)\ge l(\bar X,X) for every X\subseteq N.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circulation respecting all lower and upper arc bounds exists exactly when, across every cut, the capacity leaving the cut is at least the total mandatory lower-bound flow entering it.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both auxiliary systems use the same network and arc capacities but may have different feasible flows.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specializes binary-matrix feasibility to a common capacity for every row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let m,n\in\mathbb Z_{>0}, let a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}, and let b_1\ge\cdots\ge b_n\ge0 be integers. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all m rows have capacity a, a binary matrix meeting the column demands exists exactly when total demand is at most ma and no individual column demand exceeds m.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The witnessing flow may depend on the selected sink subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let N=S\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\mathbin{\dot\cup}T, with a(x)\ge 0 for x\in S, b(x)\ge 0 for x\in T, and arc capacities c(x,y)\ge 0. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common SDR criterion for two set families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hall-type characterization of a common SDR for two equally indexed families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal S=\{S_1,\ldots,S_n\} and \mathcal T=\{T_1,\ldots,T_n\} be families over a common indexed ground set. For X,Y\subseteq[n], let I_{\mathcal S}(X) index \bigcup_{j\in X}S_j and I_{\mathcal T}(Y) index \bigcup_{j\in Y}T_j. A common SDR for \mathcal S and \mathcal T exists if and only if, for every X,Y\subseteq[n], \[|X|+|Y|\leq n+|I_{\mathcal S}(X)\cap I_{\mathcal T}(Y)|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two indexed set families have a common SDR exactly when every pair of subfamilies satisfies the stated intersection-enhanced Hall inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\text{ a common SDR}\iff\forall X,Y\subseteq[n],\ |X|+|Y|\leq n+|I_{\mathcal S}(X)\cap I_{\mathcal T}(Y)|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Criterion for Binary Matrix Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes feasibility with upper-bounded row sums and lower-bounded column sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a_i\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0} for i=1,\ldots,m and b_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0} for j=1,\ldots,n, with b_1\ge\cdots\ge b_n. Define a_j^*=\lvert\{i:a_i\ge j\}\rvert. There exists A=(a_{ij})\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n} such that \sum_{i=1}^m a_{ij}\ge b_j for every j and \sum_{j=1}^n a_{ij}\le a_i for every i if and only if \sum_{j=1}^k b_j\le\sum_{j=1}^k a_j^* for every k=1,\ldots,n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative integer row capacities and nonincreasing column demands, a binary matrix meeting every column demand without exceeding any row capacity exists exactly when every demand prefix is bounded by the corresponding prefix of the conjugate row-capacity sequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists A\in\{0,1\}^{m\times n}:\bigl[(\forall j)\ \sum_i a_{ij}\ge b_j\ \land\ (\forall i)\ \sum_j a_{ij}\le a_i\bigr]\iff(\forall k\in\{1,\ldots,n\})\ \sum_{j=1}^k b_j\le\sum_{j=1}^k a_j^*

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Circulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible circulation with zero lower bounds and finite arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\) assign arc capacities. A capacitated circulation is a vector \(f\in\mathbb{R}^{E}\) satisfying \(0\leq f_e\leq u_e\) for every \(e\in E\) and flow conservation at every vertex: \[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}f_e=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}f_e\qquad(v\in V).\] The feasibility problem asks whether such an \(f\) exists; with zero lower bounds, the zero circulation is always feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated circulation respects every arc capacity and has equal total inflow and outflow at each vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is feasible exactly when \(0\leq f_e\leq u_e\) and flow is conserved at every vertex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong Duality and Integrality for Minimum-Cost Bounded Circulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost circulation with real arc costs and two-sided real bounds, including primal and dual integrality refinements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph and let $c,d,k:A\to\mathbb R$. Then
\[
\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}k(a)f(a): f\text{ is a circulation in }D,\ d\le f\le c\right\}
=
\max\left\{\sum_{a\in A}(y(a)d(a)-z(a)c(a)): y,z\in\mathbb R_+^A,\ \exists p:V\to\mathbb R,\ y(a)-z(a)=k(a)-p(v)+p(u)\ \forall a=(u,v)\in A\right\}.
\]
If $d$ and $c$ are integer-valued, an integer optimal circulation $f$ may be chosen. If $k$ is integer-valued, integer optimal multipliers $y,z$ may be chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a digraph with real arc costs and lower and upper bounds, the minimum cost of a bounded circulation equals the maximum dual value obtained from nonnegative lower- and upper-bound multipliers whose difference equals the reduced arc cost induced by a vertex potential. Integer bounds permit an integer optimal circulation, and integer costs permit integer optimal bound multipliers.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a circulation with }d\le f\le c
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_f\sum_{a\in A}k(a)f(a)=\max_{y,z,p}\sum_{a\in A}(y(a)d(a)-z(a)c(a)),\quad y(a)-z(a)=k(a)-p(v)+p(u)\ \forall a=(u,v);\quad c,d\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow f\text{ may be integral},\quad k\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow y,z\text{ may be integral}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-flow circulation representation and cut capacity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a capacitated source–sink maximum-flow problem as an augmented circulation and defines source–sink cuts and their capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ be a directed network with source $s$, sink $t$, and finite nonnegative capacities $u_{ij}$ on its original arcs. Set the original-arc costs and all node balances to zero, and add an artificial arc $(t,s)$ with $c_{ts}=-1$ and $u_{ts}=\infty$. The resulting circulation objective is $-x_{ts}$, so minimizing it maximizes $x_{ts}$. A cut is a set $C\subseteq\mathcal N$ with $s\in C$ and $t
otin C$, and its capacity is $\kappa(C)=\sum_{i\in C,\,j
otin C}u_{ij}$, with the sum restricted to original arcs. Every feasible augmented circulation satisfies $x_{ts}=\sum_{i\in C,\,j
otin C}x_{ij}-\sum_{i
otin C,\,j\in C}x_{ij}$, again using only original arcs in the sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow can be represented as a zero-balance circulation by adding an infinite-capacity return arc from the sink to the source with cost minus one. Minimizing circulation cost then maximizes the return-arc flow. A cut contains the source but not the sink; its capacity is the total capacity of original arcs leaving it, and flow balance makes the return-arc flow equal the net original flow crossing the cut.

C\subseteq\mathcal N,\qquad s\in C,\qquad t\notin C.
x\text{ is a feasible circulation in the augmented network.}

\min c^Tx\equiv\max x_{ts},\qquad \kappa(C)=\sum_{\substack{i\in C\j
otin C}}u_{ij},\qquad x_{ts}=\sum_{\substack{i\in C\j
otin C}}x_{ij}-\sum_{\substack{i
otin C\j\in C}}x_{ij},\quad	ext{where all cut sums use only original arcs.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Decomposition of an infeasible capacitated flow problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable-cost flow with balanced prescribed divergences that cannot all be realized within zero-lower-bound capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider $\min\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}f_{ij}(x_{ij})$ subject to divergences $y_i=s_i$ and $0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}$, where $\sum_i s_i=0$, and suppose these constraints are infeasible. A maximally feasible flow is a capacity-feasible $x$ satisfying $y_i\ge0$ for $s_i>0$, $y_i\le0$ for $s_i<0$, and $y_i=0$ for $s_i=0$, while minimizing $\sum_i|s_i-y_i|$. Such a flow $x^*$ can be found through the associated max-flow problem. Its minimal and maximal saturated cuts have arc flows fixed at $x^*_{ij}$ for every maximally feasible flow. Consequently, separable-cost minimization over all maximally feasible flows decomposes into independent feasible subproblems on $\mathcal S_{\min}$ and $\mathcal N\setminus\mathcal S_{\max}$, together with a third subproblem on $\mathcal S_{\max}\setminus\mathcal S_{\min}$ exactly when $\mathcal S_{\min}\ne\mathcal S_{\max}$; supplies are adjusted by the fixed cut-arc flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When balanced supplies and demands cannot be fully routed within capacities, a maximally feasible flow minimizes total unmet imbalance subject to the appropriate supply, demand, and transshipment divergence signs. An associated max-flow computation finds one. Its extremal saturated cuts fix their crossing flows for every maximally feasible solution and split subsequent separable-cost optimization into two independent feasible subproblems, or three when the extremal cuts differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\arg\min\left\{\sum_i|s_i-y_i|:0\le x\le c,\ y_i\operatorname{sgn}(s_i)\ge0,\ y_i=0\text{ if }s_i=0\right\},\quad\text{and the cost problem decomposes over }\mathcal S_{\min},\ \mathcal N\setminus\mathcal S_{\max},\ \text{and, if nonempty, }\mathcal S_{\max}\setminus\mathcal S_{\min}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed cut, flux, capacity, and saturation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary identities for directed cuts under lower and upper arc-flow bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q=[\mathcal S,\mathcal N\setminus\mathcal S]$ be the ordered partition induced by $\varnothing
e\mathcal S\subsetneq\mathcal N$. Define $Q^+=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal A:i\in\mathcal S,\ j
otin\mathcal S\}$ and $Q^-=\{(i,j)\in\mathcal A:i
otin\mathcal S,\ j\in\mathcal S\}$. The cut separates $s$ from $t$ if $s\in\mathcal S$ and $t
otin\mathcal S$, and it is nonempty if $Q^+\cup Q^-
e\varnothing$. For a nonempty cut, $F(Q)=\sum_{(i,j)\in Q^+}x_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in Q^-}x_{ij}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}y_i$. Given arc bounds $b_{ij}\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}$, its capacity is $C(Q)=\sum_{(i,j)\in Q^+}c_{ij}-\sum_{(i,j)\in Q^-}b_{ij}$, and every capacity-feasible flow satisfies $F(Q)\le C(Q)$. A nonempty cut is saturated with respect to $x$ when $F(Q)=C(Q)$, equivalently when every forward arc is at its upper bound and every backward arc is at its lower bound. By convention, every empty cut is saturated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directed cut is an ordered bipartition. Forward arcs leave its first side and backward arcs enter it. Its net flux equals the sum of divergences on the first side. For a capacity-feasible flow, flux does not exceed the lower–upper-bound cut capacity; equality characterizes saturation. Empty cuts are saturated by convention.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\text{ is a directed graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(Q)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal S}y_i\le C(Q),\qquad F(Q)=C(Q)\iff\left(x_{ij}=c_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in Q^+,\ x_{ij}=b_{ij}\ \forall(i,j)\in Q^-\right)\text{ for nonempty }Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Maximum-Flow Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-capacity form of max-flow integrality and cut duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with source \(s\), sink \(t\), and capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). Then there exists a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow \(f\) satisfying \(f(e)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\) for every \(e\in E\). Consequently, the common max-flow/min-cut value is an integer, and an integral maximum flow decomposes into integral multiples of directed \(s\)-\(t\) path flows together with integral directed cycle flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite network with nonnegative integer capacities has an integral maximum flow; its value is integral and admits an integral path-and-cycle decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed, with distinct \(s,t\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists f^*:\ f^*\text{ is maximum and }f^*(e)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\text{ for all }e\in E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Menger Connectivity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite directed two-terminal edge and internally vertex-disjoint forms of Menger's theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph and let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct. The maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \(G-F\) has no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path. If \(st\notin E\), the maximum number of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths pairwise disjoint outside \(\{s,t\}\) equals the minimum cardinality of a set \(X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\}\) such that \(G-X\) has no directed \(s\)-\(t\) path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed local edge connectivity equals minimum edge-separator size. If there is no arc from the source to the sink, directed local vertex connectivity equals minimum internal vertex-separator size.
assumptions_latex: \(s,t\in V\) are distinct; the vertex form additionally assumes \(st\notin E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_G(s,t)=\min\{|F|:F\subseteq E,\ G-F\text{ has no directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\), and if \(st\notin E\), then \(\kappa_G(s,t)=\min\{|X|:X\subseteq V\setminus\{s,t\},\ G-X\text{ has no directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Disjoint Path Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-capacity flow representation of directed edge-disjoint terminal paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) with terminals \(s,t\), assign capacity \(u(e)=1\) to every edge. Any family of \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths yields an integral flow of value \(k\) by summing their incidence vectors. Conversely, after deleting cycle components, every integral flow of value \(k\) decomposes into \(k\) unit path flows using no edge more than once. Hence the maximum number of edge-disjoint directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths equals the unit-capacity maximum-flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-disjoint terminal paths are exactly the path components of integral flows in the network obtained by assigning unit capacity to every edge.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and directed, with distinct terminals \(s,t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{k:\text{there are }k\text{ edge-disjoint directed }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}\}=\max\{|f|:f\text{ is feasible under }u\}\).

notation.meaning: Edge-incidence vector of a directed path.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local edge-connectivity consequence of packing edge-disjoint parity joins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an undirected graph and let \(T\subseteq V(H)\) have even cardinality. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an undirected graph contains k edge-disjoint T-joins for an even vertex set T, then every vertex t in T has some distinct vertex s joined to it by k edge-disjoint paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall t\in T\ \exists s\in V(H)\setminus\{t\}: H\text{ contains }k\text{ pairwise edge-disjoint }s\text{-}t\text{ paths}.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Packing–transversal equality for multiple set-pair path families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-disjoint path min–max equality under pairwise disjoint complements of the terminal-set pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,k$, let $S_i,T_i\subseteq V$ satisfy $S_i\cap T_i=\varnothing$. Define $U_i:=V\setminus(S_i\cup T_i)$. If $U_1,\ldots,U_k$ are pairwise disjoint, then the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint paths in $\{P:\exists i,\ P\text{ is an }S_i\text{--}T_i\text{ path}\}$ equals the minimum cardinality of an edge set intersecting every path in that family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If each source–target set pair is disjoint and the complements of their unions are pairwise disjoint, then the maximum packing of edge-disjoint admissible paths equals the minimum edge transversal of all admissible paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{|\mathcal P|:\mathcal P\text{ is a pairwise edge-disjoint subfamily of }\bigcup_{i=1}^k\mathcal P(S_i,T_i)\}=\min\{|F|:F\subseteq E,\ F\cap E(P)\ne\varnothing\ \forall P\in\bigcup_{i=1}^k\mathcal P(S_i,T_i)\}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent bi-set and path-connectivity conditions for circuits sharing two specified vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be undirected, let $s,t\in V$, and let $\ell\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$. knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Disjoint Path Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-splitting representation of internally vertex-disjoint directed paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have distinct terminals \(s,t\). Replace each internal vertex \(v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\) by vertices \(v^{\mathrm{in}},v^{\mathrm{out}}\) and a capacity-one arc \(v^{\mathrm{in}}v^{\mathrm{out}}\). Replace each original arc \(vw\) by an arc from the output copy of \(v\) to the input copy of \(w\), with terminal copies interpreted naturally and capacity at least \(|V|\). Integral flows in this split network correspond, after cycle deletion, to families of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths pairwise disjoint outside \(\{s,t\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting each internal vertex through a unit-capacity arc converts internally vertex-disjoint paths into ordinary integral flows.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph with distinct terminals \(s,t\).
Only internal vertices are required to be mutually disjoint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{k:k\text{ internally vertex-disjoint directed }s\text{-}t\text{ paths exist}\}=\operatorname{maxflow}(G^{\mathrm{split}},s,t)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Saturated Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum source side determined by residual reachability from the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a maximum flow and let \(G_f\) be its residual graph. Define \(S_{\min}\) as the set of vertices reachable from \(s\) in \(G_f\). Then \(t\notin S_{\min}\), every arc from \(S_{\min}\) to its complement is saturated by \(f\), and every arc entering \(S_{\min}\) carries zero flow. Thus \(\delta^+(S_{\min})\) is a minimum cut. Moreover, for every minimum-cut source side \(S\), one has \(S_{\min}\subseteq S\), so \(S_{\min}\) is the unique inclusion-minimal minimum-cut source side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices residually reachable from the source form the unique smallest source side among all minimum cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a maximum flow in a finite capacitated directed network.
\(G_f\) contains exactly the residual arcs of positive residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\min}=\operatorname{Reach}_{G_f}(s)\) and \(S_{\min}\subseteq S\) for every minimum-cut source side \(S\).

notation.meaning: Residual graph of the maximum flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Saturated Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum source side determined by reverse residual reachability to the sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a maximum flow with residual graph \(G_f\). Let \(R_t\) be the set of vertices from which \(t\) is reachable in \(G_f\), and put \(S_{\max}=V\setminus R_t\). Then \(s\in S_{\max}\), \(t\notin S_{\max}\), every arc leaving \(S_{\max}\) is saturated by \(f\), and every arc entering \(S_{\max}\) carries zero flow. Hence \(\delta^+(S_{\max})\) is a minimum cut. Every minimum-cut source side \(S\) satisfies \(S\subseteq S_{\max}\), making \(S_{\max}\) uniquely inclusion-maximal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing vertices that can residually reach the sink gives the unique largest source side among all minimum cuts.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a maximum flow in a finite capacitated directed network.
\(G_f\) contains exactly the residual arcs of positive residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{\max}=V\setminus\{v:v\leadsto t\text{ in }G_f\}\) and \(S\subseteq S_{\max}\) for every minimum-cut source side \(S\).

notation.meaning: Vertices from which the sink is residually reachable.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremal-Cut Lattice Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributive lattice of minimum-cut source sides under inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite capacitated directed network, let \(\mathcal C\) be the collection of source sides of minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cuts. If \(A,B\in\mathcal C\), submodularity of directed cut capacity gives \(A\cap B\in\mathcal C\) and \(A\cup B\in\mathcal C\). Therefore \((\mathcal C,\subseteq)\) is a distributive lattice with meet \(A\wedge B=A\cap B\) and join \(A\vee B=A\cup B\). Its bottom and top elements are respectively the residual-reachability sets \(S_{\min}\) and \(S_{\max}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-cut source sides are closed under intersection and union, forming a distributive lattice with unique smallest and largest cuts.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite, directed, and has nonnegative capacities.
\(\mathcal C\) consists of source sides of minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal C,\cap,\cup)\) is a distributive lattice with bottom \(S_{\min}\) and top \(S_{\max}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extremal saturated cuts under union and intersection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremal structure of saturated source–sink cuts associated with a fixed optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an optimal max-flow solution $x^*$. Let $\mathcal F$ be the family of source-side sets $\mathcal S$ for which $[\mathcal S,\mathcal N\setminus\mathcal S]$ is saturated with respect to $x^*$ and separates $s$ from $t$. Then $\bigcup_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S$ defines the maximal saturated separating cut, while $\bigcap_{\mathcal S\in\mathcal F}\mathcal S$ defines the minimal saturated separating cut. These two cuts coincide if and only if the saturated separating cut is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed optimal flow, the union of all saturated-cut source sides gives the maximal saturated separating cut, and their intersection gives the minimal one. They coincide exactly when that cut is unique.

knowledge_statements.title: Ford–Fulkerson Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic residual augmenting-path method with arbitrary path selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed network \((G,u,s,t)\) and initialize \(f=0\). While the residual graph \(G_f\) contains a directed \(s\)-\(t\) path \(P\), set \(\Delta=\min_{e\in P}u_f(e)\) and augment \(f\) by \(\Delta\) along forward residual arcs and by \(-\Delta\) along reverse residual arcs. If no residual \(s\)-\(t\) path exists, stop and output \(f\); this output is a maximum flow. If all capacities are integral, every augmentation has \(\Delta\ge 1\), so the method terminates after at most \(|f^*|\) augmentations, where \(f^*\) is a maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from zero, repeatedly augment along any residual source-to-sink path. If no such path remains, the flow is maximum; integral capacities guarantee termination after at most the maximum-flow value many augmentations.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and capacities are nonnegative.
The finite-termination bound additionally assumes \(u(e)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) for every \(e\in E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_f\text{ has no }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\Rightarrow f\text{ is maximum}\); with integral capacities and \(f=0\) initially, the number of augmentations is at most \(|f^*|\).

notation.meaning: Residual graph of the current flow.
Residual capacity of a residual arc.
Bottleneck residual capacity of the selected path.
A maximum flow, with \(|f^*|\) denoting its value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Potential duality and optimality criterion for minimum-cost k-braids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-capacity fixed-value minimum-cost flow duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let D=(V,A), let c:A\to\mathbb R_+, and let k be a feasible positive integer. For a potential \pi:V\to\mathbb R_+ satisfying \pi(s)=0\le\pi(v)\le\pi(t), define c_\pi(uv)=c(uv)-\pi(v)+\pi(u). Then the minimum cost of a k-braid from s to t is
\[
\max_\pi\left\{k\pi(t)+\sum_{uv\in A:\,c_\pi(uv)<0}c_\pi(uv)\right\}.
\]
A k-braid z is minimum-cost if and only if some potential \pi satisfies, for every uv\in A,
\[
c_\pi(uv)>0\Rightarrow z(uv)=0,\qquad c_\pi(uv)<0\Rightarrow z(uv)=1.
\]
If c is integer-valued, an optimal potential may be chosen integer-valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonnegative arc costs, the minimum cost of k edge-disjoint source-to-sink paths equals a maximum over node potentials. A k-braid is optimal exactly when every positive-reduced-cost arc is unused and every negative-reduced-cost arc is saturated at one. Integer costs admit an integer optimal potential.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph with distinguished }s,t
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{z\in\mathcal B_k}cz=\max_\pi\left(k\pi(t)+\sum_{c_\pi(e)<0}c_\pi(e)\right),\quad z\text{ is optimal}\iff\exists\pi\text{ satisfying the reduced-cost conditions};\ c\in\mathbb Z^A\Rightarrow\pi\text{ may be integral}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path maximum-flow procedure using forward and backward labeling scans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a capacitated network \(N=(s,t,V,A,b)\), initialize \(f:=0\). Repeatedly initialize a labeling search at \(s\). When scanning a labeled vertex \(x\), label each unlabeled vertex reachable from \(x\) through an unsaturated forward arc and each unlabeled vertex whose positive-flow arc enters \(x\), recording the corresponding forward or backward predecessor. If \(t\) is labeled, augment \(f\) along the resulting augmenting path and restart; if the scan list becomes empty without labeling \(t\), terminate and output \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Begin with zero flow. Repeatedly search from the source through unsaturated arcs in their forward direction and positive-flow arcs in reverse. If the sink is reached, augment along the labeled path and restart; otherwise stop and return the current flow.
assumptions_latex: N=(s,t,V,A,b)\text{ is a capacitated flow network}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure terminates its search when }t\text{ cannot be labeled and outputs the current flow }f.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Scaling Augmentation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary residual-capacity scaling for integral maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral capacities, initialize \(f=0\) and \(\Delta\) as the largest power of two not exceeding \(U=\max_{e\in E}u(e)\). During a \(\Delta\)-phase, retain only residual arcs with capacity at least \(\Delta\); while this subgraph contains an \(s\)-\(t\) path, augment along such a path by its full residual bottleneck. When no path remains, replace \(\Delta\) by \(\Delta/2\). Stop after completing the \(\Delta=1\) phase. The output is a maximum flow; the standard implementation uses \(O(|E|\log U)\) augmentations and \(O(|E|^2\log U)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict augmentations to arcs above a decreasing power-of-two threshold, ending at one; this gives a maximum integral flow with logarithmically many phases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{aug}}=O(|E|\log U)\), \(T=O(|E|^2\log U)\), and the returned flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-Based Augmenting Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting paths constructed using feasible vertex-price labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a feasible flow \(f\) and vertex prices \(p:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) with \(p(t)=0\) and \(p(v)\le p(w)+1\) for every residual arc \(vw\). Initialize \(f=0\) and choose prices equal to residual distances to \(t\), using \(+\infty\) for unreachable vertices. Construct an augmenting path using admissible arcs satisfying \(p(v)=p(w)+1\). If a reached vertex has no admissible outgoing residual arc, relabel it to \(1+\min\{p(w):vw\text{ is residual}\}\). Augment on reaching \(t\); stop when \(p(s)=+\infty\), and output \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible vertex prices identify admissible residual arcs; path construction alternates admissible advances with relabeling until augmentation or a maximum-flow certificate results.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite and has nonnegative capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(s)=+\infty\Rightarrow G_f\text{ has no directed }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\Rightarrow f\text{ is maximum}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Advance-retreat implementation driven by residual-distance labels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize x:=0, compute exact residual-distance labels d, and set i:=s. While d(s)<n, advance from i along an admissible residual arc (i,j), setting \operatorname{pred}(j):=i and i:=j. Upon reaching t, recover the predecessor path P, set \delta:=\min\{r_{uv}:(u,v)\in P\}, augment \delta units on P, and reset i:=s. If i has no admissible arc, set d(i):=\min\{d(j)+1:(i,j)\in A(i),\ r_{ij}>0\}; when i\ne s, retreat to \operatorname{pred}(i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with zero flow and exact residual-distance labels. Repeatedly advance along admissible residual arcs; on reaching the sink, augment by the path bottleneck and return to the source. At a dead end, relabel the current node using the minimum neighboring residual label plus one and retreat to its predecessor. Stop when the source label reaches n.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a capacitated }s\text{-}t\text{ network with }n=|N|.
r_{ij}\text{ denotes residual capacity, and admissible arcs are defined by the maintained distance labels.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d(s)\ge n\text{ is the stopping condition after repeated advance, retreat, and bottleneck-augmentation operations.}

knowledge_statements.title: Irrational-Capacity Nontermination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of arbitrary-path Ford–Fulkerson termination beyond commensurable capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Ford–Fulkerson with arbitrary augmenting-path choices need not terminate when capacities are irrational. The failure mechanism is an infinite feasible augmentation sequence with bottlenecks \(\Delta_k>0\) such that \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\Delta_k<\infty\): every finite iterate still has a residual \(s\)-\(t\) path, while the flow values converge to a limit strictly below the maximum-flow value. Classical finite-network constructions choose capacities involving an irrational ratio and paths that implement a Euclidean-algorithm recurrence, producing infinitely many positive remainders. Thus finite termination requires a path rule or a discrete capacity unit, not merely finiteness of the network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With irrationally related capacities, adversarial augmenting paths can generate infinitely many shrinking augmentations and converge below the maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite but permits irrational capacities.
Augmenting paths may be selected arbitrarily.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists (G,u)\ \exists(P_k)_{k\ge1}:\ \Delta_k>0,\ \sum_k\Delta_k<\operatorname{maxflow}(G,u),\text{ and Ford--Fulkerson never terminates}\).

notation.meaning: Augmenting path selected at iteration k.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite directed network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), capacities \(u:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and feasible flow \(f\), repeat: compute residual distances \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,v)\); if \(t\) is unreachable, output \(f\). Otherwise form the level graph \(L_f=(V,\{(v,w)\in E_f:d(w)=d(v)+1\})\), find a blocking flow \(g\) in \(L_f\), and augment \(f\) by \(g\). Each phase strictly increases the residual distance from \(s\) to \(t\), so at most \(|V|-1\) blocking-flow phases occur. A standard current-arc implementation constructs each blocking flow in \(O(|V||E|)\) time, giving total running time \(O(|V|^2|E|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dinic repeatedly augments by a blocking flow in the residual level graph. At most |V|-1 phases occur, and a standard O(|V||E|)-time blocking-flow implementation gives total running time O(|V|^2|E|).

knowledge_statements.title: Karzanov Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preflow-based construction of blocking flows in an acyclic layered network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=(V,A)\) be an acyclic residual level network. Initialize zero flow and process internal vertices by forward pushes along admissible outgoing arcs, permitting temporary positive excess. When a vertex can send no further flow, process its remaining excess backward along incoming flow-carrying arcs; delete vertices or arcs that cannot participate further. Continue until every internal vertex is balanced and every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains a saturated arc. The resulting feasible flow is blocking in \(L\) and may be used as one phase of a layered maximum-flow method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karzanov-style procedures construct a blocking flow by forward preflow pushes, backward excess balancing, and elimination of unusable layered-network elements.
assumptions_latex: \(L=(V,A)\) is a finite acyclic level network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is feasible and every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(L\) contains an arc saturated by \(g\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a simple digraph with \(n:=|V(G)|\) and \(m:=|E(G)|\), let \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_+\), and define \(u_{\max}:=\max\{u(e):e\in E(G)\}\). Fujishige's algorithm computes a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow in \(O(mn\log u_{\max})\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a simple directed graph with n vertices, m edges, and nonnegative integral capacities, Fujishige's algorithm correctly computes a maximum flow in O(mn log u_max) time, where u_max is the largest edge capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Fujishige's algorithm returns a maximum }s\text{-}t\text{ flow in }O(mn\log u_{\max})\text{ time.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity-scaling residual-network algorithm for nonnegative integral capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a network \((G,u,s,t)\) with \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_+\), initialize \(f=0\) and \(\alpha=\max_{e\in E(G)}u(e)\). For each scale, start with \(v_1=s\), accumulate for every unselected vertex \(w\) the residual capacities \(u_f(v_i,w)\) from scanned vertices, and make \(w\) eligible once its accumulation is at least \(\alpha\). If no vertex is eligible, replace \(\alpha\) by \(\lfloor\alpha/2\rfloor\), terminating when \(\alpha=0\). Otherwise select eligible vertices until \(t\) is selected; set \(\beta(t)=\alpha\) and propagate this amount backward through residual arcs from earlier selected vertices, augmenting each arc by \(\min\{\beta(v_i),u_f(p,v_i)\}\). Repeat the scale search. The output is a maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the zero flow and the largest capacity as a scaling threshold. At each threshold, select vertices whose accumulated incoming residual capacity from previously selected vertices reaches the threshold. If the sink is reached, send one threshold unit backward through the selected residual arcs and repeat. If no vertex is eligible, halve the threshold; stop when it becomes zero. The resulting flow is maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a maximum }s\text{-}t\text{ flow.}

knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Capacity Blocking Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dinic phase bound for directed networks whose original arcs have unit capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed network with \(u(e)=1\) on every original arc, Dinic's algorithm computes each blocking flow in \(O(|E|)\) time. After \(k\) phases the residual \(s\)-\(t\) distance exceeds \(k\). Combining this distance growth with the edge-disjoint structure of residual augmenting paths yields at most \(O(|E|^{1/2})\) phases. Consequently, a maximum flow is computable in \(O(|E|^{3/2})\) time in the adjacency-list RAM model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On directed unit-capacity networks, linear-time blocking-flow phases and a square-root phase bound give Dinic running time O(E^{3/2}).

notation.meaning: RAM running time of Dinic's algorithm

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Tree Acceleration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic-tree implementation of blocking-flow phases for maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a layered blocking-flow algorithm, represent the current forest of admissible paths by a dynamic-tree data structure supporting path-minimum residual capacity, path augmentation, linking, and cutting in \(O(\log |V|)\) amortized time. Batched path operations then implement a blocking-flow phase in \(O(|E|\log |V|)\) time. Since residual source–sink distance strictly increases between phases, at most \(|V|-1\) phases occur, giving total time \(O(|V||E|\log |V|)\) in the comparison-based RAM model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic trees batch path bottleneck and augmentation operations, yielding O(VE log V) time for layered blocking-flow maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: The residual network is finite and directed.

knowledge_statements.title: Layered Network Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual level graph used by shortest-augmenting-path blocking-flow methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible flow \(f\), let \(G_f=(V,E_f)\) be its residual network and define \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_f}(s,v)\), with \(d(v)=+\infty\) when \(v\) is unreachable. The layered network is \[L_f=\bigl(V,\{(v,w)\in E_f:d(v)<+\infty,\ d(w)=d(v)+1\}\bigr),\] with the residual capacities inherited from \(G_f\). It is acyclic, every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path in it has exactly \(d(t)\) arcs, and these paths are precisely the shortest residual augmenting paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The layered network retains residual arcs advancing one breadth-first level; it is acyclic and contains exactly the shortest residual source–sink paths.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is a feasible flow in a finite directed network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_f\) is acyclic and its \(s\)-\(t\) paths are exactly the shortest \(s\)-\(t\) paths of \(G_f\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the level graph induced by exact residual distances to the sink and records its shortest-path structure and optional pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a flow \(x\), let \(d(i)\) be the exact distance from node \(i\) to the sink in the residual network \(G(x)\). The layered network contains the residual arcs \((i,j)\) satisfying \(d(i)=d(j)+1\). Consequently, every source--sink path in the layered network is a shortest source--sink path in \(G(x)\). Arcs contained in no such path may be deleted. With \(V_k=\{i:d(i)=k\}\), every retained arc is directed from some \(V_k\) to \(V_{k-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a given flow, compute exact residual distances to the sink and retain residual arcs whose distance decreases by one. Every source–sink path in this layered network is shortest in the residual network. Arcs on no source–sink path may be deleted, and every retained arc goes from layer k to layer k−1.
assumptions_latex: x\text{ is a flow with residual network }G(x).
d(i)\text{ is the exact distance from }i\text{ to the sink in }G(x).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i,j)\in A_L\iff (i,j)\in A(G(x))\text{ and }d(i)=d(j)+1;\quad \text{every }s\text{--}t\text{ path in }G_L\text{ is shortest in }G(x).

knowledge_statements.title: Blocking-Flow Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saturated-arc certificate that a layered-network flow is blocking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\) be a feasible \(s\)-\(t\) flow in a finite layered network \(L=(V,A)\). Form the subgraph \(H_g\) from arcs having positive residual capacity after routing \(g\). The reachability set \(S=\{v:v\text{ is reachable from }s\text{ in }H_g\}\) is a verifiable blocking-flow certificate when \(t\notin S\): every arc of \(L\) leaving \(S\) is saturated, hence every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains a saturated arc. Conversely, if every directed \(s\)-\(t\) path contains a saturated arc, then \(t\notin S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual unreachability of the sink certifies that every layered source–sink path contains a saturated arc, so the flow is blocking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\text{ is blocking}\iff t\notin S\).

notation.meaning: positive-residual-capacity subgraph after routing the flow
vertices reachable from the source in that subgraph

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward augmenting paths and maximal layered-network flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines layered-network flow maximality and distinguishes it from global maximum-flow optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N=(s,t,V,A,b)\) be a layered network and let \(g\) be a flow in \(N\). An augmenting path with respect to \(g\) is forward if it uses no backward arcs. The flow \(g\) is maximal, not necessarily maximum, if and only if there is no forward augmenting path in \(N\) with respect to \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a layered network, an augmenting path is forward when it uses no backward arc. A flow is maximal, which does not mean maximum, exactly when no forward augmenting path remains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is maximal}\iff\nexists\text{ a forward augmenting path in }N\text{ with respect to }g.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance Labeling and Admissible Residual Edge
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Labeling objects used by push–relabel maximum-flow algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,s,t)$ be a network, let $f$ be an $s$-$t$ preflow, and set $n:=|V(G)|$. A distance labeling is a function $\psi:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_+$ satisfying $\psi(t)=0$, $\psi(s)=n$, and $\psi(v)\leq\psi(w)+1$ for every $(v,w)\in E(G_f)$. An edge $e=(v,w)\in E(\overleftrightarrow G)$ is admissible if and only if $e\in E(G_f)$ and $\psi(v)=\psi(w)+1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a preflow, a distance labeling assigns nonnegative integer labels with sink label zero, source label equal to the number of vertices, and a label difference of at most one across every residual edge. A bidirected edge is admissible exactly when it is residual and its tail label is one greater than its head label.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi\text{ is a distance labeling iff the stated conditions hold, and }(v,w)\text{ is admissible iff }(v,w)\in E(G_f)\text{ and }\psi(v)=\psi(w)+1.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Push–relabel operation specialized to two-arc admissible paths in a bipartite residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given node \(i\), if an admissible residual arc \((i,j)\) and then an admissible residual arc \((j,k)\) exist, push \(\delta=\min\{e(i),r_{ij},r_{jk}\}\) units along \(i-j-k\). If \((i,j)\) is admissible but no admissible \((j,k)\) exists, replace \(d(j)\) by \(\min\{d(k)+1:(j,k)\in A(j),\ r_{jk}>0\}\). If no admissible \((i,j)\) exists, replace \(d(i)\) by \(\min\{d(j)+1:(i,j)\in A(i),\ r_{ij}>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at i, push the maximum permitted amount along an admissible two-arc residual path i-j-k. If the second admissible arc is unavailable, relabel j; if the first is unavailable, relabel i.

e(i)\text{ denotes excess, }r_{uv}\text{ residual capacity, and }d\text{ a distance label}

knowledge_statements.title: Generic Preflow–Push
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic push–relabel algorithm for directed maximum flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the preflow by saturating arcs leaving \(s\), set \(h(s)=|V|\), and set \(h(v)=0\) for \(v\ne s\). While an active vertex \(v\notin\{s,t\}\) has excess \(e(v)>0\), push \(\delta=\min\{e(v),u_f(v,w)\}\) on any residual arc \((v,w)\) with \(h(v)=h(w)+1\). If no such arc exists, relabel \(v\) by \(h(v)=1+\min\{h(w):(v,w)\in E_f\}\). When no active internal vertex remains, the preflow is a feasible maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generic push–relabel repeatedly sends excess along admissible residual arcs and raises blocked vertex labels until the preflow becomes a maximum flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed capacitated network.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(v)=0\) for every \(v\notin\{s,t\}\), and the resulting flow is maximum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines push state updates, saturating and nonsaturating pushes, and relabeling in generic preflow–push.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A push of \(\delta\) units from \(i\) to \(j\) performs \[e(i)\leftarrow e(i)-\delta,\quad r_{ij}\leftarrow r_{ij}-\delta,\quad e(j)\leftarrow e(j)+\delta,\quad r_{ji}\leftarrow r_{ji}+\delta.\] The push is saturating if \(\delta\) equals the forward residual capacity before the update and nonsaturating otherwise. Under the standard choice \(\delta=\min\{e(i),r_{ij}\}\), a nonsaturating push makes \(e(i)=0\). A relabel operation increases \(d(i)\) to create an admissible outgoing residual arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A push transfers excess from one vertex to another while decreasing forward residual capacity and increasing reverse residual capacity. It is saturating when it exhausts the forward residual capacity. With the standard push amount, a nonsaturating push clears the sending vertex's excess. Relabeling increases a distance label to create an admissible arc.
assumptions_latex: (i,j)\text{ is a residual arc and the push amount }\delta\text{ is feasible.
\delta=\min\{e(i),r_{ij}\}\text{ for the conclusion about a nonsaturating push clearing }e(i).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (e(i),r_{ij},e(j),r_{ji})\leftarrow(e(i)-\delta,r_{ij}-\delta,e(j)+\delta,r_{ji}+\delta).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Nodes and Valid Push–Relabel Labellings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity and distance-label definitions for the generic preflow–push method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a preflow \(x\), a node \(v\in V\setminus\{r,s\}\) is active if and only if \(f_x(v)>0\). Consequently, a preflow is a flow if and only if it has no active nodes. With \(n=|V|\), a vector \(d\in(\mathbb Z_+\cup\{\infty\})^V\) is a valid labelling with respect to \(x\) if \(d(r)=n\), \(d(s)=0\), and \(d(v)\le d(w)+1\) for every arc \(vw\in E(G(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An internal node is active exactly when it has positive excess, and a preflow is a flow exactly when it has no active nodes. A valid label gives the source value n and the sink value zero and satisfies the stated one-step inequality on every residual arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\text{ is valid with respect to }x\iff d(r)=n,\ d(s)=0,\ \text{and }d(v)\le d(w)+1\ \forall vw\in E(G(x)).

Set \(x_e=u_e\) for every arc \(e\) with tail \(r\), set \(x_e=0\) for every other arc, set \(d(r)=n\), and set \(d(v)=0\) for every \(v\ne r\). Then \(x\) is a feasible preflow and \(d\) is a valid labelling with respect to \(x\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions and the push-preservation property for the generic preflow–push maximum-flow method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with source \(r\), sink \(s\), capacities \(u\), and \(0\le x\le u\), use the convention \(u_{wv}=x_{wv}=0\) when \(vw\in E\) and \(wv\notin E\). The auxiliary digraph \(G(x)\) contains \(vw\) if and only if \(x_{wv}>0\) or \(x_{vw}<u_{vw}\), and its residual capacity is \(\widetilde u_{vw}=u_{vw}-x_{vw}+x_{wv}\). The vector \(x\) is a preflow if \(f_x(v)\ge0\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{r,s\}\), and it is feasible when also \(0\le x\le u\). If \(\widetilde u_{vw}>0\), \(f_x(v)>0\), and \(0\le\varepsilon\le\min\{\widetilde u_{vw},f_x(v)\}\), pushing \(\varepsilon\) units from \(v\) to \(w\) produces another feasible preflow. If both orientations are original arcs, this push is implemented by decreasing \(x_{wv}\) by \(\varepsilon'=\min\{\varepsilon,x_{wv}\}\) and increasing \(x_{vw}\) by \(\varepsilon-\varepsilon'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The residual digraph has a forward arc whenever unused forward capacity or cancellable reverse flow exists, with residual capacity equal to their sum. A feasible preflow obeys capacities but permits nonnegative excess at internal nodes. A push bounded by both the residual capacity and the tail's excess preserves feasible-preflow status; antiparallel flow is canceled first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'\text{ obtained by the push is a feasible preflow.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local operations and label invariants for a validly labelled preflow residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x$ be a preflow with residual graph $G(x)$ and valid labelling $d$. Then $d(v)\le d_x(v,s)$ and $d(v)-n\le d_x(v,r)$; in particular, $d(v)\ge n$ implies $d_x(v,s)=\infty$. A residual arc $vw$ from an active vertex $v$ is admissible when $d(v)=d(w)+1$, and pushes are performed only on admissible arcs. If $v$ is active and has no admissible outgoing residual arc, relabel it by $d(v)\leftarrow\min\{d(w)+1:vw\in E(G(x))\}$. Both an admissible push and this relabel operation preserve validity of the labelling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a validly labelled preflow, labels give lower bounds on residual distances to the sink and source. Excess is pushed only along residual arcs descending by one label. If an active vertex has no such arc, its label is raised to one plus the smallest label of a residual out-neighbor; these operations preserve label validity.

G(x)\text{ is the residual graph of }x
v\text{ is active when the push or relabel rule is applied}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run generic push–relabel with a FIFO queue \(Q\) initially containing all active internal vertices. Remove the vertex \(v\) at the head and discharge it by valid admissible pushes and relabels until \(e(v)=0\). Whenever a push changes an internal vertex \(w\ne v\) from zero excess to positive excess, append \(w\) to \(Q\) if it is not already present. Continue until \(Q\) is empty. The output is a maximum flow; with standard current-arc bookkeeping, the FIFO variant has worst-case running time \(O(|V|^3)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: FIFO push–relabel fully discharges active vertices in queue order and computes a maximum flow in O(|V|^3) worst-case time.
