knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\) and \(D=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). A transportation instance is unbalanced when \(S\ne D\). Under exact constraints \(\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\) and \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\), its feasible set is empty: summing the row equations yields \(\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}=S\), whereas summing the column equations yields \(\sum_{i,j}x_{ij}=D\). A usable unbalanced model must therefore relax some equalities or introduce variables, such as dummy shipments, that absorb the difference \(\lvert S-D\rvert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is unbalanced when total supply differs from total demand; exact transportation equalities are then infeasible without augmentation or relaxation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\) and \(D=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\). If \(S>D\), add a dummy destination \(0\) with demand \(S-D\), permit a dummy shipment \(x_{i0}\ge 0\) from every origin \(i\), and set its unit cost to \(c_{i0}=p_i\). The augmented balance equations identify \(x_{i0}\) with unused supply at \(i\), so the added objective term is \(\sum_{i\in I}p_i x_{i0}\). If \(D>S\), add a dummy origin \(0\) with supply \(D-S\), permit \(x_{0j}\ge 0\) to every destination \(j\), and set \(c_{0j}=q_j\). Then \(x_{0j}\) represents unmet demand at \(j\), and the added objective term is \(\sum_{j\in J}q_j x_{0j}\). Thus, after interpreting the applicable exact real-side constraints together with unused-supply or unmet-demand variables, the balanced augmentation has exactly the real transportation cost plus the prescribed linear imbalance penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Penalty-priced dummy shipments represent linear costs for unused supply when supply is excessive and for unmet demand when demand is excessive.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given finite origin and destination sets \(I\) and \(J\), supplies \(a_i\), demands \(b_j\), route capacities \(u_{ij}\), and unit costs \(c_{ij}\), the capacitated transportation problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\ \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=a_i\ \text{ for every }i\in I,\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=b_j\ \text{ for every }j\in J,\ 0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\ \text{ for every }(i,j)\in I\times J\right\}.\] A route may be forbidden by setting \(u_{ij}=0\). Aggregate balance \(\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{j\in J}b_j\) is necessary but need not be sufficient, because route capacities can prevent realization of the required row and column sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacitated transportation minimizes shipment cost subject to exact supplies and demands and an upper bound on every origin-destination route.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the model hierarchy and states the reduction to single-source–single-sink minimum-cost flow, including its feasibility and path-cost qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A transshipment problem assigns each node \(i\) an imbalance \(b_i\) and requires \(\sum_j x_{ji}-\sum_j x_{ij}\ge b_i\), with \(b_i<0\), \(b_i>0\), and \(b_i=0\) denoting supply, demand, and transshipment nodes, respectively. Arcs have linear costs and are uncapacitated unless finite capacities are specified. A Hitchcock--Koopmans transportation problem is the specialization to a bipartite graph \(G=(S,T,A)\), with supply nodes in \(S\), demand nodes in \(T\), and arcs directed from \(S\) to \(T\); the assignment problem further has equally many supply and demand nodes and \(b_i\in\{-1,1\}\). Feasibility requires \(-\sum_{b_i<0}b_i\ge\sum_{b_i>0}b_i=:v\). If every directed supply-to-demand path has nonnegative cost, adjoining a source \(s\) with zero-cost arcs \((s,i)\) of capacity \(-b_i\) to supply nodes and a sink \(t\) with zero-cost arcs \((j,t)\) of capacity \(b_j\) from demand nodes converts the problem to a conventional minimum-cost flow of value \(v\), whose optimum yields a transshipment solution. If negative-cost supply-to-demand paths exist, lower bounds on the arcs \((j,t)\) are required. Conversely, a minimum-cost flow of prescribed value is a capacitated transshipment problem, and capacitated transshipment can be reduced to uncapacitated Hitchcock--Koopmans transportation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment problem replaces ordinary flow conservation by prescribed node imbalances: negative, positive, and zero imbalances identify supply, demand, and transshipment nodes. Transportation is its bipartite supply-to-demand specialization, and assignment is the unit-supply/unit-demand case with equally many nodes on both sides. Total supply must cover total demand. When all supply-to-demand paths have nonnegative cost, adding a super-source and super-sink with the stated zero-cost capacities reduces transshipment to a minimum-cost flow of value equal to total demand; negative-cost paths require lower bounds on the demand-to-sink arcs. Minimum-cost flow is conversely a capacitated transshipment problem, and capacitated transshipment admits a reduction to uncapacitated transportation.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the stated super-source/super-sink reduction without lower bounds, every directed supply-to-demand path has nonnegative cost.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Under these conditions, a minimum-cost }s\text{-}t\text{ flow of value }v\text{ yields an optimal transshipment solution; the stated model specializations and converse reductions hold.}

Create an origin copy and destination copy of every vertex, with supply \(M+b_v^+\) and demand \(M+b_v^-\). Permit \(y_{vw}\) with capacity \(u_{vw}\) and cost \(c_{vw}\) for every original arc, and permit a zero-cost diagonal cell \(y_{vv}\). Then \(x_{vw}=y_{vw}\) on original arcs, while diagonal cells absorb unused row and column mass. Subtracting each column equation from its corresponding row equation gives the original balance equation, establishing a cost-preserving correspondence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transshipment as a network-flow model and its transportation reformulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies the transshipment problem as a minimum-cost network-flow problem and records the stated direct solution method and transportation-model conversions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A transshipment problem seeks a minimum-cost feasible shipping pattern among origins where goods are available, destinations where goods are required, and intermediate nodes where goods are neither supplied nor demanded but may pass through. It is a network-flow problem that can be solved directly by the network simplex algorithm. The source also states that it can be converted into a transportation problem by tracing shortest paths between each origin--destination pair or by adding buffer stocks at suitable nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transshipment problem minimizes shipping cost over a network with supply origins, demand destinations, and zero-net-supply intermediate nodes. It can be solved directly by network simplex or converted to transportation form using origin–destination shortest paths or suitable buffer stocks.
assumptions_latex: \text{The network contains origins, destinations, and intermediate transshipment nodes.}
\text{Intermediate transshipment nodes have neither available nor required goods.}
\text{The shipping pattern is feasible and incurs shipping costs.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The least-cost shipping problem is a network-flow problem admitting network-simplex solution and the stated transportation reformulations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bound on Optimal Transshipment Under Positive Loop Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A boundedness result used in the transportation–transshipment equivalence construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j=L\), and the sum of the costs \(c_{ij}\) around every loop in the network is positive. If an optimal solution exists, then, in any optimal solution, each transshipped amount \(x_{jj}\) is bounded by \[x_{jj}\leq \sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j=L.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When total supply and total demand equal L and every network loop has positive total cost, each amount transshipped through a node in any existing optimal solution is at most L.
assumptions_latex: \text{The sum of }c_{ij}\text{ around every network loop is positive.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall j,\quad x_{jj}\leq \sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j=L\quad\text{in any optimal solution.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a feasible basic transportation plan whose basic cells form a spanning tree of the bipartite graph. Compute potentials satisfying \(\alpha_i+\beta_j=c_{ij}\) on every basic cell and reduced costs \(r_{ij}=c_{ij}-\alpha_i-\beta_j\) on every nonbasic cell. If every nonbasic reduced cost satisfies \(r_{ij}\ge 0\), stop and output the current plan. Otherwise, choose a nonbasic entering cell with \(r_{ij}<0\). Adding it to the tree creates a unique alternating cycle. Increase flow on the plus cells and decrease flow on the minus cells by \(\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the minimum current flow on a minus cell. Remove a limiting minus cell, apply the specified anti-cycling rule when \(\theta=0\) or a tie occurs, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transportation simplex pivots around alternating cycles of a bipartite tree basis until every nonbasic reduced cost is nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network connectivity and componentwise transshipment decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity is expressed using chains of joined arcs without imposing an unsupported orientation requirement; decomposition requires absence of cross-component coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network \(G=(V,A)\) is connected if, for every \(i,j\in V\), there is a sequence \(i=v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_m=j\) such that each consecutive pair \(v_{r-1},v_r\) is joined by an arc. If \(G\) consists of separate connected components and the transshipment formulation contains no constraints or objective terms coupling different components, then the problem decomposes into independent transshipment subproblems, one for each component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network is connected when every pair of nodes can be linked by a chain of arcs. If a transshipment network has separate connected components and no cross-component coupling, its problem separates into independent component subproblems.
assumptions_latex: \text{For decomposition, the connected components have no intercomponent arcs or other model coupling.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The transshipment problem decomposes into independent subproblems on the connected components.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A single-commodity transshipment on \(G=(V,E)\) assigns one scalar flow \(x_e\ge0\) to each arc. With the convention that \(b_v\) is required net outflow, feasibility means \[\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e=b_v\qquad\text{for every }v\in V,\] equivalently \(Ax=b\). Vertices with \(b_v>0\) supply the commodity, vertices with \(b_v<0\) demand it, and vertices with \(b_v=0\) only transship it. When costs \(c_e\) are specified, the linear-cost model minimizes \(\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e\) over these feasible flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Single-commodity transshipment routes one homogeneous scalar flow so that each node's net outflow equals its prescribed supply or demand.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a network incidence matrix. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the net-outflow incidence convention, the linear minimum-cost flow problem is \[\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.\] This is exactly a bounded single-commodity transshipment problem with arc costs \(c_e\), prescribed node supplies and demands \(b_v\), and arc bounds \([\ell_e,u_e]\). Conversely, every such transshipment model has this minimum-cost flow form. Lower bounds may be removed by writing \(x=\ell+z\), which yields \(0\le z\le u-\ell\), adjusted balance \(Az=b-A\ell\), and an objective differing by the constant \(c^\top\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-cost bounded single-commodity transshipment is precisely minimum-cost flow in node-incidence form; shifting by lower bounds adjusts capacities and balances and adds an objective constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Flow Interface

children.title: Square Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment models with equal cardinalities on the two bipartite sides.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite sets with \(\lvert I\rvert=\lvert J\rvert=n\).
Every pair \((i,j)\in I\times J\) is allowed and has a finite cost \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible square assignment is a perfect bipartite matching, equivalently a permutation matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete one-to-one assignment with equally many agents and tasks.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 9. Minimum Cost Flows p. 215

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets satisfying \(\lvert I\rvert=\lvert J\rvert=n\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}\) be the cost of assigning \(i\in I\) to \(j\in J\). The square assignment problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:\ \sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\ \text{ for every }i\in I,\ \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\ \text{ for every }j\in J,\ x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\ \text{ for every }(i,j)\in I\times J\right\}.\] Every feasible solution is a permutation matrix: there is a bijection \(\pi:I\to J\) such that \(x_{i,\pi(i)}=1\) for every \(i\in I\). Conversely, every such bijection is feasible. Thus the model is the unit-supply, unit-demand balanced transportation problem and is equivalent to a minimum-cost perfect matching in the complete bipartite graph on vertex classes \(I\) and \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Square assignment matches equally many agents and tasks bijectively while minimizing total cost; its feasible solutions are permutation matrices.
knowledge_statements.title: Square Assignment

children.title: Rectangular Assignment
children.top_down_role: Assignment models with unequal bipartite-side cardinalities.

knowledge_statements.title: Rectangular Assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the regime in which every vertex of the smaller side is assigned injectively to the larger side.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\) and \(R\) be finite sets with \(|L|\le |R|\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for \((i,j)\in L\times R\). A rectangular assignment is a binary vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{L\times R}\) satisfying
\[\sum_{j\in R}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in L),\qquad \sum_{i\in L}x_{ij}\le 1\quad(j\in R).\]
The minimum-cost rectangular assignment problem minimizes \(\sum_{i\in L}\sum_{j\in R}c_{ij}x_{ij}\) over these vectors. Thus every vertex of \(L\) is assigned, while vertices of \(R\) may remain unused.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rectangular assignment injectively matches every vertex on the smaller side to a distinct vertex on the larger side. The minimum-cost problem selects such an assignment of least total cost.
assumptions_latex: All costs \(c_{ij}\) are finite real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible solutions are precisely injections from \(L\) into \(R\), encoded by \(x\).

notation.meaning: Cost of assigning left vertex i to right vertex j.
Binary indicator that pair (i,j) is selected.

children.title: Dummy-Vertex Completion
children.top_down_role: Completion of a rectangular instance to square form using dummy vertices.

knowledge_statements.title: Dummy-Vertex Completion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pads a rectangular assignment instance to a square perfect-assignment instance without changing costs on genuine assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(|L|=m\le n=|R|\). Add a dummy set \(D\) of size \(n-m\), put \(L'=L\mathbin{\dot\cup}D\), and define \(c'_{ij}=c_{ij}\) for \(i\in L\) and \(c'_{dj}=0\) for \(d\in D\). Every perfect assignment on \(L'\times R\) restricts to a rectangular assignment on \(L\times R\); conversely, every rectangular assignment extends by matching the unused vertices of \(R\) bijectively to \(D\). Corresponding solutions have equal objective value, so restriction and extension preserve optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding enough zero-cost dummy vertices makes a rectangular instance square; perfect assignments then project to rectangular assignments with unchanged cost.
assumptions_latex: Dummy edges are permitted to every vertex of \(R\) and have zero cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rectangular optimum equals the perfect-assignment optimum on \(L'\times R\).

notation.meaning: Cost matrix extended by zero-cost dummy rows.

children.title: Partial-Assignment Regime
children.top_down_role: Rectangular settings where unmatched vertices remain part of the intended model.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial-Assignment Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines assignments of a prescribed cardinality without requiring either vertex class to be saturated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, let \(c_e\in\mathbb R\), and fix an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le\min\{|L|,|R|\}\). A partial assignment of cardinality \(k\) is a vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfying
\[\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le1\quad(v\in L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R),\qquad \sum_{e\in E}x_e=k.\]
Its cost is \(\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\). The regime permits unmatched vertices on both sides and may be infeasible when \(G\) contains no matching of size \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A partial assignment is a matching containing exactly k edges; vertices on either side may remain unmatched.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible vectors encode exactly the matchings of cardinality \(k\) in \(G\).

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment as Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents a cardinality-constrained bipartite assignment as an integral minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a bipartite graph \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\), construct a network with arcs \((s,i)\), \((i,j)\), and \((j,t)\) for \(i\in L\), \((i,j)\in E\), and \(j\in R\). Give every arc capacity \(1\), assign cost \(c_{ij}\) only to \((i,j)\), and require flow value \(k\). Each integral flow corresponds bijectively to a cardinality-\(k\) assignment through \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\), and its flow cost equals \(\sum_{(i,j)\in E}c_{ij}x_{ij}\). Hence minimum-cost integral flows and minimum-cost partial assignments correspond.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Send k flow units through source–left–right–sink paths. Integral flows select k vertex-disjoint assignment edges with identical total cost.
assumptions_latex: The required flow value is an integer \(k\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum-cost integral flows of value \(k\) correspond cost-preservingly to minimum-cost assignments of cardinality \(k\).

notation.meaning: Flow on the arc representing assignment edge (i,j).

knowledge_statements.title: Hungarian Primal–Dual Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the square minimization form using feasible dual labels, equality edges, and augmenting-tree label updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a square cost matrix \(c\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Initialize \(u,v\) with \(u_i+v_j\le c_{ij}\), and maintain a matching using only equality edges \(u_i+v_j=c_{ij}\). From an unmatched left vertex, grow an alternating tree with reachable sets \(S,T\). If no augmenting equality edge exists, set
\[\Delta=\min_{i\in S,\,j\notin T}(c_{ij}-u_i-v_j),\]
replace \(u_i\) by \(u_i+\Delta\) for \(i\in S\) and \(v_j\) by \(v_j-\Delta\) for \(j\in T\), and continue. Augment when possible; output the matching when it is perfect.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hungarian method alternates equality-graph augmentations with dual-label updates until a perfect matching satisfying complementary slackness is obtained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output perfect matching minimizes \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}c_{i,\pi(i)}\).

notation.meaning: Feasible left and right dual labels.
Left and right vertices reached by the alternating tree.
Minimum dual slack crossing from S to the unreached right side.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite convergence of the integer-cost Hungarian algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-termination guarantee based on integral reduced-cost or dual-objective progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite \(m\times m\) assignment problem with integer costs, suppose a nonoptimal Hungarian iteration covers all current zero cells using \(\bar k<m\) row or column lines, lets \(c_0\) be the minimum uncovered reduced cost, and applies the standard reduced-matrix adjustment. The associated dual objective increases by \(c_0(m-\bar k)\ge 1\). When a minimum cover of size \(k<m\) is used, the sum of the reduced costs decreases by \(m(m-k)c_0>0\). Because the reduced costs remain nonnegative and the dual objective is bounded above, only finitely many adjustments can occur, and termination yields an optimal assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer assignment costs, each nonoptimal Hungarian adjustment makes positive integral progress. The dual objective rises by at least one, while a minimum-cover adjustment strictly decreases the sum of nonnegative reduced costs. Thus the method terminates after finitely many adjustments at an optimal assignment.
assumptions_latex: \bar k<m\ \text{lines cover all current zero cells}
\text{the standard Hungarian reduced-matrix adjustment is applied}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta D=c_0(m-\bar k)\ge 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{finite termination at an optimal assignment}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hungarian algorithm for square minimum-cost assignment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Row-column reduction and repeated zero-cover adjustments for an m-by-m assignment cost matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(C\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\), first subtract each row minimum from its row and then each resulting column minimum from its column. Repeatedly cover all zeros of the reduced matrix with the minimum number \(k\) of row or column lines. If \(k=m\), an optimal assignment can be selected among the zero cells. If \(k<m\), let \(c_0\) be the smallest uncovered entry; subtract \(c_0\) from every uncovered entry, add \(c_0\) to every twice-covered entry, leave entries covered once unchanged, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hungarian algorithm performs row and column reductions, covers all zeros with as few row or column lines as possible, and stops when m lines are required. Otherwise it subtracts the smallest uncovered value from uncovered entries, adds it to twice-covered entries, and repeats; at the stopping condition an optimal assignment is available among the zeros.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=m\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the zero cells contain an optimal complete assignment}.

knowledge_statements.title: Auction Assignment Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the forward auction algorithm for square maximum-weight assignment with additive auction increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input weights \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb R\), prices \(p_j=0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). While some bidder \(i\) is unassigned, choose \(j^*\in\arg\max_j(a_{ij}-p_j)\). Let \(V_1=a_{ij^*}-p_{j^*}\) and \(V_2=\max_{j\ne j^*}(a_{ij}-p_j)\). Raise \(p_{j^*}\) by \(V_1-V_2+\varepsilon\), assign \(i\) to \(j^*\), and unassign its previous bidder, if any. Stop when all bidders are assigned. The output satisfies \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness; for integral weights, it is optimal when \(0<\varepsilon<1/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unassigned bidders repeatedly claim their best net-valued object and raise its price beyond their second-best option; sufficiently small epsilon gives an optimal integral assignment.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\ge2\) bidders and \(n\) objects, with finite weights \(a_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination yields an \(\varepsilon\)-complementary-slack assignment; if \(a_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\) and \(0<\varepsilon<1/n\), the assignment is maximum-weight.

notation.meaning: Best and second-best net values for the active bidder.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epsilon-Complementary Slackness and the Tie-Cycling Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines approximate complementary slackness for partial assignments and records the zero-increment cycling failure of the naive auction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $\epsilon>0$, a partial assignment and price vector $p$ satisfy $\epsilon$-complementary slackness if every assigned pair $(i,j)$ satisfies $a_{ij}-p_j\ge\max_{k\in A(i)}\{a_{ik}-p_k\}-\epsilon$. In the naive auction, a tie between best objects can make $\gamma_i=0$, so prices need not increase and the iteration can cycle indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon-complementary slackness assigns every currently assigned person an object whose net value is within epsilon of that person's best available net value. With no perturbation, tied best objects can produce zero bids and a nonterminating auction cycle.
assumptions_latex: (i,j)\text{ ranges over assigned pairs in a partial assignment.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_{ij}-p_j\ge\max_{k\in A(i)}\{a_{ik}-p_k\}-\epsilon\quad\forall(i,j)\text{ assigned};\qquad \gamma_i=0\text{ under a best-value tie can permit nontermination.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Candidate-list bid calculation for the assignment auction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bid-computation subroutine for an assignment auction using cached candidate objects and their recorded prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an unassigned person \(i\). Examine \(\operatorname{Cand}(i)\) from its beginning, discarding entries \((j,p'_j)\) for which \(p'_j<p_j\), until the list ends or a second entry satisfying \(p'_j=p_j\) is reached. If two such entries are found, let \(j_i\) be the first, discard all preceding list contents through that first entry, and bid for \(j_i\) at price level \(p_{j_i}+\epsilon\). If the list ends, empty it and scan \(A(i)\) to determine a maximum-value object \(j_i\), the prescribed next-best value \(w_i\), and all objects other than \(j_i\) tied at \(w_i\); record those tied objects with their current prices and bid for \(j_i\) at the prescribed level \(b_{ij_i}\). In either case, assign \(i\) to \(j_i\) and break any prior assignment of \(j_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an unassigned person, scan the cached candidate list and remove stale entries. If two candidates still have current recorded prices, bid on the first at its current price plus epsilon and retain the list beginning with the second. Otherwise, clear the cache, recompute the best and next-best values over the admissible objects, cache the other objects tied for next best, and submit the prescribed bid for the best object. The bidder receives the selected object and any former assignment of that object is broken.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{Cand}(i)\text{ contains pairs }(j,p'_j)\text{ of candidate objects and recorded prices.}
p_j\text{ is the current price of object }j.
A(i)\text{ is the set of objects admissible for person }i.
w_i\text{ and }b_{ij_i}\text{ are defined by the referenced auction formulas.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Person }i\text{ is assigned to the selected object }j_i\text{ at the computed bid level, displacing any prior assignee of }j_i.

children.title: Cardinality B-Matching Reduction
children.top_down_role: Flow representations for maximizing the size of a bipartite b-matching.

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality B-Matching Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces maximum-cardinality bipartite b-matching to maximum flow using vertex-capacity arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) have integer vertex bounds \(b_v\ge0\) and integer edge capacities \(u_e\ge0\). Construct arcs \((s,i)\) of capacity \(b_i\), arcs \((i,j)\) of capacity \(u_{ij}\), and arcs \((j,t)\) of capacity \(b_j\). For every integral flow, set \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\). Flow conservation gives \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\), and every integral capacitated b-matching extends uniquely to such an internal flow. Moreover, its cardinality \(\sum_{e\in E}x_e\) equals the flow value. Thus maximum cardinality equals maximum flow value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertex bounds become source- and sink-side capacities, edge multiplicities become middle-arc capacities, and b-matching cardinality becomes flow value.
assumptions_latex: All bounds \(b_v\) and capacities \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum b-matching cardinality equals the maximum \(s\)-\(t\) flow value in the constructed network.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted B-Matching Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translates fixed-cardinality weighted bipartite b-matching into minimum-cost flow by negating edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the bipartite network with capacities \(b_i,u_{ij},b_j\), assign cost \(-w_{ij}\) to each middle arc \((i,j)\) and zero cost to all other arcs. Require an \(s\)-\(t\) flow of value \(k\). Under the correspondence \(x_{ij}=f_{ij}\),
\[\operatorname{cost}(f)=-\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}x_{ij}.\]
Consequently, an integral minimum-cost flow of value \(k\) corresponds exactly to a maximum-weight capacitated b-matching of cardinality \(k\), provided such a flow exists. Integrality of capacities permits an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating edge weights turns maximum-weight b-matching of a fixed cardinality into minimum-cost flow of the same value.
assumptions_latex: The bipartite instance has integral capacities \(b_v,u_e\ge0\).
A feasible b-matching of prescribed cardinality \(k\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Minimum flow cost equals the negative maximum weight among b-matchings of cardinality \(k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Capacity Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes bipartite vertex-incidence bounds as capacities adjacent to the flow source and sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite bipartite graph \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\), introduce a source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Give \((s,i)\) capacity \(b_i\) for every \(i\in L\), give \((j,t)\) capacity \(b_j\) for every \(j\in R\), and orient each edge \(\{i,j\}\in E\) as an arc \((i,j)\) of capacity \(u_{ij}\). Every feasible flow satisfies
\[0\le f_{ij}\le u_{ij},\qquad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}f_{ij}\le b_i,\qquad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}f_{ij}\le b_j.\]
Conversely, every vector \(x\) satisfying these nonnegativity, edge-capacity, and vertex-incidence bounds extends uniquely on the source and sink arcs by setting \(f_{si}=\sum_jx_{ij}\), \(f_{ij}=x_{ij}\), and \(f_{jt}=\sum_ix_{ij}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Left and right vertex bounds become capacities on the adjacent source and sink arcs. Vectors satisfying those bounds and the edge capacities correspond to feasible flows.
assumptions_latex: All vertex and edge capacities are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flow feasibility on the encoded network is equivalent to the b-matching vertex-incidence inequalities together with nonnegativity and edge capacities.

notation.meaning: Capacity of the middle arc representing edge (i,j).

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Translation Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates fixed-cardinality weight translation from objectives that optimize cardinality or permit the empty matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cost substitution \(c_e=-w_e\) preserves a weighted b-matching objective only after the flow value is fixed, or after a separate construction explicitly models variable value. It does not by itself encode maximum cardinality, nor does fixed value encode the convention that an empty matching may dominate negative-weight edges. For example, in a graph consisting of one edge \(e\) with \(w_e=-1\), the unrestricted maximum-weight b-matching is empty with weight \(0\), whereas requiring flow value \(1\) selects \(e\) with weight \(-1\). Therefore cardinality, fixed-value weight, and unrestricted-weight objectives require distinct translations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating weights is correct for fixed flow value, but it does not automatically preserve maximum-cardinality or unrestricted maximum-weight conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reduction must encode the intended cardinality convention separately from the identity \(c_e=-w_e\).

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated Bipartite B-Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines integral bipartite b-matchings with both vertex-incidence bounds and edge-multiplicity capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph. Given integer vertex capacities \(b_v\ge0\) and integer edge capacities \(u_e\ge0\), a capacitated bipartite b-matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\) satisfying
\[0\le x_e\le u_e\quad(e\in E),\qquad \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\quad(v\in L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R).\]
Its cardinality is \(\sum_{e\in E}x_e\), and, for edge weights \(w_e\), its weight is \(\sum_{e\in E}w_ex_e\). The value \(x_e\) is the permitted multiplicity of edge \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated bipartite b-matching assigns a nonnegative integer multiplicity to each edge while respecting every edge capacity and each endpoint's total incidence capacity.
assumptions_latex: The data \(b_v\) and \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities define the feasible capacitated bipartite b-matchings.

notation.meaning: Maximum total multiplicity incident to vertex v.

knowledge_statements.title: B-Matching Integrality Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transfers network-flow integrality to the capacitated bipartite b-matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, with integer bounds \(b_v,u_e\ge0\). Define
\[P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E}:0\le x_e\le u_e,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le b_v\text{ for every }v\in L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R\right\}.\]
Every vertex of \(P\) is integral. Equivalently, for every linear objective \(w\in\mathbb R^{E}\), there is an optimal solution over \(P\) belonging to \(\mathbb Z^{E}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer vertex and edge capacities make the finite bipartite b-matching polytope integral, so every linear objective has an integral optimum.
assumptions_latex: All bounds \(b_v\) and \(u_e\) are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every extreme point of \(P\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z^{E}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph with weights \(w:V\to\mathbb R\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is closed when \((i,j)\in A\) and \(i\in S\) imply \(j\in S\). Construct a network with source \(s\), sink \(t\), an arc \((s,i)\) of capacity \(w_i\) when \(w_i>0\), an arc \((i,t)\) of capacity \(-w_i\) when \(w_i<0\), and every dependency arc \((i,j)\) assigned capacity \(M\), where \(M>\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i\). If \((C,\bar C)\) is any minimum \(s\)-\(t\) cut and \(S=C\cap V\), then \(S\) is a maximum-weight closed set and \[\max_{S'\subseteq V:\,S'\text{ closed}}\sum_{i\in S'}w_i=\sum_{i:w_i>0}w_i-\operatorname{mincut}(s,t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any minimum source-sink cut, the original vertices on its source side form a maximum-weight dependency-closed selection; its weight equals total positive vertex weight minus the minimum-cut capacity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite project set, let \(p_i\in\mathbb R\) be the net profit of project \(i\), and let \(R\subseteq P\times P\) encode prerequisites: \((i,j)\in R\) means selecting \(i\) requires selecting \(j\). With binary variables \(x_i\), the project-selection problem is \[\max\left\{\sum_{i\in P}p_i x_i:x_i\le x_j\ \text{for every }(i,j)\in R,\ x_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}.\] Its feasible selected sets \(S=\{i:x_i=1\}\) are exactly the closed sets of \((P,R)\). Consequently, applying the maximum-closure cut construction with vertex weights \(p_i\) yields an optimal project portfolio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projects with arbitrary net profits are selected subject to prerequisite implications. Feasible portfolios are precisely closed vertex sets, so a maximum-closure minimum-cut construction finds an optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Dependency Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed implication networks for feasible binary selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A selection-dependency network is a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\) together with binary selection variables \(x_i\) for \(i\in V\), where an arc \((i,j)\in A\) imposes the implication \(x_i\le x_j\). A binary vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{V}\) is dependency-feasible precisely when all these inequalities hold. Equivalently, its support \(S(x)=\{i\in V:x_i=1\}\) is closed under outgoing arcs. Directed paths encode transitive implications: if a directed path leads from \(i\) to \(j\), then every dependency-feasible vector satisfies \(x_i\le x_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each directed arc means that selecting its tail requires selecting its head. Feasible selections are outgoing-arc-closed sets, and directed paths express transitive requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is dependency-feasible if and only if \(S(x)\) is closed in \(D\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with integral transit times \(\tau_e\ge1\), capacities \(u_e\ge0\), and integer horizon \(T\ge0\). Its discrete time expansion has vertices \((v,\theta)\) for \(v\in V\) and \(\theta\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\). For every \(e=(v,w)\in E\) and integer \(\theta\) satisfying \(\theta+\tau_e\le T\), it contains a transit arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((w,\theta+\tau_e)\) of capacity \(u_e\). For every \(v\in V\) and \(\theta<T\), it contains a holdover arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+1)\) of capacity \(+\infty\). With identical terminal supplies, demands, and boundary conventions in the two models, static flow conservation at time-expanded vertices is equivalent to temporal conservation with unrestricted waiting. Hence feasible discrete temporal flows through horizon \(T\) correspond to feasible static flows in the expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copy each vertex at every integer time, shift every transit arc by its travel time, and add infinite-capacity holdover arcs for unrestricted waiting. With matching terminal and boundary conventions, static flows in this network represent discrete temporal flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Time Flow Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate-function formulation of deterministic flow over time with transit delays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc \(e=(v,w)\) of a finite network, let \(f_e:[0,T)\to\mathbb R_+\) be a measurable departure-rate function, with \(0\le f_e(\theta)\le u_e\) almost everywhere and constant transit time \(\tau_e\ge0\). Flow entering \(e\) at time \(\theta\) reaches \(w\) at time \(\theta+\tau_e\). At every intermediate vertex \(v\), feasibility with storage requires, for all \(t\in[0,T]\), \[\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}\int_0^{(t-\tau_e)_+}f_e(\theta)\,d\theta-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}\int_0^t f_e(\theta)\,d\theta\ge0.\] Equality describes zero inventory; the nonnegative difference is inventory at \(v\) at time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous-time temporal flow uses measurable arc departure rates. Delayed cumulative inflow minus cumulative outflow is nonnegative inventory, with equality when intermediate storage is forbidden.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities and transit times are deterministic and time-independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed delayed cumulative-balance inequalities characterize conservation with unrestricted nonnegative intermediate storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Holdover-Arc Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-expanded arcs representing one-period waiting at a vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a discrete time-expanded network with layers \(0,\ldots,T\), a holdover arc at vertex \(v\) and time \(\theta<T\) is the arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+1)\). A flow amount on this arc represents material retained at \(v\) throughout period \([\theta,\theta+1)\). Its capacity is the permitted inventory carried across that period: it is \(+\infty\) for unrestricted waiting, a finite value \(b_{v,\theta}\) for bounded storage, and \(0\) when waiting at \(v\) during that period is forbidden.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A holdover arc joins consecutive time copies of one vertex. Its flow is stored inventory, and its capacity specifies whether waiting is unrestricted, bounded, or forbidden.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Flow on \(((v,\theta),(v,\theta+1))\) equals inventory carried at \(v\) across period \(\theta\).

knowledge_statements.title: Storage-Capacity Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite inventory bounds in discrete or continuous temporal networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_v(t)\) denote inventory stored at vertex \(v\) at time \(t\), after arrivals and departures are accounted for under a fixed boundary convention. A storage-capacity function \(b_v(t)\in\mathbb R_+\cup\{+\infty\}\) imposes the feasibility condition \[0\le I_v(t)\le b_v(t)\qquad\text{for every admissible time }t.\] In a discrete time expansion, this condition is represented by assigning capacity \(b_v(\theta)\) to the holdover arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+1)\). Thus storage bounds are vertex-time constraints in the temporal model and ordinary arc-capacity constraints in its expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inventory at each vertex and time must lie between zero and its storage bound. In a time expansion, that bound becomes the corresponding holdover-arc capacity.
assumptions_latex: Inventory is measured using a fixed arrival-departure boundary convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le I_v(t)\le b_v(t)\), represented discretely by a holdover-arc capacity.

notation.meaning: inventory at vertex v and time t
storage capacity at vertex v and time t

children.title: Transit-Time Structure
children.top_down_role: Temporal displacement induced when flow traverses an arc.

assumptions_latex: Transit times are deterministic and time-independent.
Flow does not disappear while traversing an arc.
No flow is initially in transit, equivalently \(f_e(\theta)=0\) for \(\theta<0\).
For the discrete time-expansion statement, \(\theta\) and \(\tau_e\) are integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Departures at \(\theta\) enter the head at \(\theta+\tau_e\), and in continuous time this gives the displayed shifted cumulative-arrival function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic temporal arcs transport departures to transit-time-shifted arrival states.

source_refs.locator: Section 12. Networks with Transit Times p. 92

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e=(v,w)\) be a physical arc with deterministic, time-independent transit time \(\tau_e\ge0\). A departure on \(e\) at time \(\theta\) arrives at \(w\) at time \(\theta+\tau_e\). In a discrete time expansion, when \(\theta\) and \(\tau_e\) are integral and both endpoint times lie in the horizon, this is represented by a transit arc from \((v,\theta)\) to \((w,\theta+\tau_e)\). In continuous time, let \(f_e:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R_+\) be the departure-rate function and assume \(f_e(\theta)=0\) for \(\theta<0\). The cumulative amount delivered through \(e\) by time \(t\ge0\) is then \[A_e(t)=\int_0^{(t-\tau_e)_+}f_e(\theta)\,d\theta.\] Thus capacity constrains departures, while conservation at the head uses the transit-time-shifted arrival process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic transit arc shifts every departure forward by its transit time. The discrete expansion links the corresponding integral time states, while the continuous model obtains cumulative arrivals by shifting the departure-rate integral, assuming no flow is initially in transit.

children.title: Waiting–Transit Interaction
children.top_down_role: How waiting choices interact with traversal delays in time-expanded representations.

assumptions_latex: Time and transit times are integral.
Waiting occurs only through available holdover arcs.
Residual capacity \(r_a\) is defined relative to a fixed feasible flow in the time expansion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Waiting \(k\) periods before using \(e\) changes the arrival time from \(\theta+\tau_e\) to \(\theta+k+\tau_e\), and a path-flow amount \(q\) is admissible when each path arc has residual capacity at least \(q\).

notation.meaning: time of arrival at the tail vertex
residual capacity of expanded arc a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition of waiting and transit in a discrete time-expanded network.

source_refs.locator: Section 9.7. Flows Over Time p. 236

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose flow reaches vertex \(v\) at integral time \(\theta\), waits for \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\) periods, and then enters arc \(e=(v,w)\) with integral transit time \(\tau_e\). In the time expansion this motion is represented by a path of \(k\) successive holdover arcs followed by the transit arc from \((v,\theta+k)\) to \((w,\theta+k+\tau_e)\). Its arrival time is therefore \(\theta+k+\tau_e\). Relative to a fixed feasible expanded flow, let \(r_a\) be the residual capacity of each arc \(a\) on this path. A path-flow amount \(q>0\) can be routed along the path when \(r_a\ge q\) for every path arc and \(\theta+k+\tau_e\le T\), where \(T\) is the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waiting advances flow through holdover arcs before transit begins, so waiting time and transit time add. A specified path-flow amount can use this route when every holdover and transit arc has enough residual capacity and the resulting arrival is within the horizon.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible Flow and Maximum-Flow Linear Program
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a capacitated static source-to-sink flow and its value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,A)$ be directed, let $s,t\in V$, and let $c_{ij}\ge 0$ for every $(i,j)\in A$. A feasible $s$-$t$ flow is a vector $x$ satisfying $0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij}$ and flow conservation at every $i\in V\setminus\{s,t\}$. Its value $v$ is the net outflow from $s$, equivalently the net inflow to $t$. The maximum-flow problem is the linear program $\max v$ subject to these constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible directed flow respects every arc capacity and conserves flow at all nodes except the source and sink. Its value is the source's net outflow, equal to the sink's net inflow, and maximum flow is obtained by maximizing this value subject to those linear constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\left\{v:0\le x_{ij}\le c_{ij},\ \sum_jx_{ji}=\sum_jx_{ij}\ \forall i\notin\{s,t\},\ v=\sum_jx_{sj}-\sum_jx_{js}=\sum_jx_{jt}-\sum_jx_{tj}\right\}

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Horizon Maximum Dynamic Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink maximum flow delivered by a prescribed deadline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have source \(s\), sink \(t\), arc rate capacities \(u_e\ge0\), transit times \(\tau_e\ge0\), and horizon \(T>0\). A feasible dynamic flow consists of nonnegative measurable departure rates satisfying arc capacities and temporal conservation at every vertex in \(V\setminus\{s,t\}\), with waiting permitted and zero initial inventory. Its fixed-horizon value is the cumulative flow arriving at \(t\) by time \(T\), namely \[\operatorname{val}_T(f)=\sum_{e\in\delta^-(t)}\int_0^{(T-\tau_e)_+}f_e(\theta)\,d\theta-\sum_{e\in\delta^+(t)}\int_0^T f_e(\theta)\,d\theta.\] The maximum dynamic-flow problem maximizes \(\operatorname{val}_T(f)\) over all feasible dynamic flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a deadline, maximize the net amount that has reached the sink by that time, subject to rate capacities, transit delays, and temporal conservation.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and transit times are deterministic and constant.
Waiting is permitted and initial intermediate inventory is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimum is \(\max\{\operatorname{val}_T(f):f\text{ is a feasible dynamic flow}\}\).

notation.meaning: net flow delivered to the sink by T

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_T\) be the set of directed \(s\)-\(t\) paths \(P\) satisfying \(\tau(P)<T\), where \(\tau(P)=\sum_{e\in P}\tau_e\). Choose path rates \(x_P\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T:e\in P}x_P\le u_e\) for every arc \(e\). The associated temporally repeated flow dispatches rate \(x_P\) along path \(P\) at every departure time \(\theta\in[0,T-\tau(P))\), with each downstream arc entered after the cumulative transit time of the preceding arcs. This dynamic flow is feasible and delivers value \[\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T}(T-\tau(P))x_P.\] Consequently, the best temporally repeated flow is represented by the static path-flow problem \[\max\left\{\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T}(T-\tau(P))x_P:\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_T:e\in P}x_P\le u_e\ \text{for every }e,\ x_P\ge0\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every source-sink path that can reach the sink before the horizon, a static path rate is dispatched continuously until its last deadline-feasible departure. Its delivered amount is the rate multiplied by the horizon minus the path transit time, and the best repeated flow is a weighted static path-flow optimization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimality of a Temporally Repeated Flow at a Fixed Horizon
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-horizon maximum dynamic flow induced by the designated static flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a horizon of \(p\) periods, the static flow \(r_{p+1}\) generates a temporally repeated dynamic flow that is maximal among all dynamic flows over that horizon. Its value is \[v(p)=(p+1)v_{p+1}-\sum_{(x,y)}a(x,y)f_{p+1}(x,y),\] where \(v_{p+1}\) is the value of \(r_{p+1}\). The dynamic cut \(\mathcal C\) defined by (9.17) is minimum for the same horizon.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Cut Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum cuts in a time expansion certify discrete dynamic-flow optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integral-horizon temporal network and its finite time expansion, augmented by a supersource connected to admissible source-time copies and a supersink connected from sink-time copies representing deliveries by the horizon. Let \(f\) be a feasible static flow in this expansion and let \((S,\bar S)\) be a supersource-supersink cut. If \[\operatorname{val}(f)=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}\ell_a,\] where \(\ell_a\) and \(u_a\) are expanded-arc lower and upper capacities, then weak duality and static max-flow min-cut imply that \(f\) is maximum. Under the temporal-flow correspondence, the cut is a verifiable certificate that the represented dynamic flow is optimal through the prescribed horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A time-expanded cut whose capacity equals a feasible dynamic flow’s delivered value certifies optimality by static max-flow min-cut duality.
assumptions_latex: Temporal flows and expanded static flows use the same boundary convention.
Every expanded arc has capacities \(0\le\ell_a\le u_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equality between expanded-flow value and cut capacity certifies fixed-horizon dynamic-flow optimality.

knowledge_statements.title: Quickest Source–Sink Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time, single-commodity quickest-flow formulation for a prescribed source–sink demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a directed network have source \(s\), sink \(t\), arc capacities \(u_a\ge 0\), transit times \(\tau_a\ge 0\), and demand \(Q\ge 0\). A feasible flow over time with horizon \(T\) consists of measurable entrance rates \(f_a:[0,T)\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfying \(f_a(\theta)\le u_a\) almost everywhere, temporal flow conservation at every intermediate vertex, and no entrance after \(T-\tau_a\) when arrival by \(T\) is required. The quickest source–sink flow problem is
\[T^*=\inf\{T\ge0:F_t(T)\ge Q\},\]
where \(F_t(T)\) is cumulative net flow arriving at \(t\) by time \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find the least horizon by which a capacity- and transit-time-feasible dynamic flow can deliver the prescribed amount from source to sink.
assumptions_latex: Flow may be held at intermediate vertices unless explicitly forbidden.

notation.meaning: entrance rate into arc a at time theta
cumulative net arrival at the sink by T

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed network with arc capacities \(u_a\ge 0\) and transit times \(\tau_a\ge 0\), and let \(b:V\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), where \(b_v>0\) is supply and \(b_v<0\) is demand. For a horizon \(T\), a feasible dynamic transshipment consists of capacity-feasible arc entrance rates and inventories \(I_v(\theta)\ge 0\) satisfying temporal balance, with initial inventories \(I_v(0)=b_v^+:=\max\{b_v,0\}\) and terminal inventories \(I_v(T)=(-b_v)^+:=\max\{-b_v,0\}\). The quickest-transshipment value is \[T^*=\inf\{T\ge 0:\text{there exists a feasible dynamic transshipment realizing }b\text{ by }T\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the common horizon in which all initially available supplies can be transported to their specified demand vertices while respecting capacities, transit times, and nonnegative intermediate inventories.

knowledge_statements.title: Earliest-Arrival Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink earliest-arrival criterion over a fixed maximum horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a source \(s\), sink \(t\), and horizon \(T\). For a feasible flow over time \(f\), let \(F_t^f(\theta)\) be its cumulative net arrival at \(t\) by time \(\theta\). The flow \(f^*\) is an earliest-arrival flow through horizon \(T\) if
\[F_t^{f^*}(\theta)\ge F_t^f(\theta)\qquad\text{for every feasible }f\text{ and every }\theta\in[0,T].\]
This simultaneous dominance at every intermediate time is stronger than merely maximizing the amount delivered at \(T\) or minimizing the completion time for one prescribed demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An earliest-arrival flow maximizes cumulative sink arrivals simultaneously at every time up to the chosen horizon.
assumptions_latex: All compared flows use the same temporal network and horizon \(T\).
Cumulative arrivals are measured under the same boundary-time convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_t^{f^*}(\theta)=\max_f F_t^f(\theta)\) for every \(\theta\in[0,T]\).

notation.meaning: cumulative net sink arrival under flow f by theta

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Horizon Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-horizon search using monotonicity of dynamic-flow feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an integer demand specification and a feasibility oracle \(\mathcal F(T)\), first find bounds \(L<U\) with \(\mathcal F(L)=\mathrm{false}\) and \(\mathcal F(U)=\mathrm{true}\), doubling \(U\) if necessary. While \(U-L>1\), set \(M=\lfloor(L+U)/2\rfloor\); if \(\mathcal F(M)\) is true, replace \(U\) by \(M\), and otherwise replace \(L\) by \(M\). Return \(U\) and a feasible flow supplied by the final oracle call. Correctness uses the monotonicity implication
\[\mathcal F(T)\Longrightarrow\mathcal F(T+1),\]
which holds when a feasible solution may wait or remain idle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary-search the integer horizon using a monotone feasibility test, returning the smallest feasible horizon and its flow.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility is monotone under extension of the horizon.
The oracle returns a witnessing flow whenever feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U=\min\{T\in\mathbb Z_+:\mathcal F(T)=\mathrm{true}\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed network, let \(T\in\mathbb Z_+\), and let every arc \(a\in A\) have a transit time \(\tau_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 1}\). For \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let \(x_{a,t}\ge 0\) be flow dispatched onto arc \(a\) at the beginning of period \(t\), subject to \(x_{a,t}\le u_{a,t}\). Given initial inventories \(I_{v,0}\), external net supplies \(b_{v,t}\), and nonnegative inventories \(I_{v,t}\), dynamic balance requires \[I_{v,t+1}=I_{v,t}+b_{v,t}+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_{a,t+1-\tau_a}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_{a,t}\] for every \(v\in V\) and \(t=0,ldots,T-1\), where variables with indices outside \(\{0,\ldots,T-1\}\) are interpreted as zero. A feasible collection \((x,I)\) satisfying these constraints and the prescribed terminal inventory or demand requirements is a dynamic transshipment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic transshipment dispatches flow through capacitated arcs with positive integral delays while maintaining nonnegative, time-indexed inventories and satisfying the prescribed terminal requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Flow over Time
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost, discrete-time dynamic transshipment over a fixed finite horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given horizon \(T\), arc-time costs \(c_{a,t}\), holding costs \(h_{v,t}\), capacities, transit times, supplies, demands, and admissible terminal inventories, the minimum-cost flow-over-time problem chooses a feasible dynamic transshipment \((x,I)\) minimizing
\[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\sum_{a\in A}c_{a,t}x_{a,t}+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{v\in V}h_{v,t}I_{v,t}.\]
Feasibility includes delayed flow balance, arc-time capacity bounds, nonnegative inventories, and the stated terminal regime. If storage is disallowed, the corresponding intermediate inventories are fixed to zero; if holding is free, the relevant \(h_{v,t}\) vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a feasible flow and inventory trajectory minimizing total time-indexed transportation and storage cost.
assumptions_latex: The horizon and all temporal data are finite.
Costs are linear and all decision variables are continuous.
Dynamic balance uses the prescribed arc transit times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,I^*)\in\arg\min\{\sum_{a,t}c_{a,t}x_{a,t}+\sum_{v,t}h_{v,t}I_{v,t}:(x,I)\text{ feasible}\}\).

notation.meaning: unit transportation cost on arc a in period t

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite horizon \(T\), form a time-expanded graph with vertex copies \((v,t)\) for every \(v\in V\) and \(t=0,\ldots,T\). Each original arc \(a=(v,w)\) and departure time \(t\) satisfying \(t+\tau_a\le T\) induces an arc \(((v,t),(w,t+\tau_a))\) with the corresponding capacity and cost. When storage is permitted, add holdover arcs \(((v,t),(v,t+1))\). Assign supplies and demands to the appropriate time copies, including the initial and terminal inventory requirements. Static flow conservation at the time copies is then the dynamic inventory-balance system. Consequently, feasible dynamic transshipments through \(T\) correspond bijectively to feasible static transshipments in the time-expanded network, with equal linear cost when the induced arc costs match the dynamic costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Copy each vertex at every discrete time and represent delayed transport and permitted storage by ordinary arcs; with matching boundary balances, static flows in this network correspond exactly to dynamic flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiperiod Transportation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time transportation model with period-specific shipments and carried inventory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be supply locations, \(D\) demand locations, and \(t=1,\ldots,T\). A multiperiod transportation plan chooses shipments \(x_{ij,t}\ge0\) and inventories \(I_{i,t},J_{j,t}\ge0\) satisfying
\[I_{i,t}=I_{i,t-1}+s_{i,t}-\sum_{j\in D}x_{ij,t},\qquad J_{j,t}=J_{j,t-1}+\sum_{i\in S}x_{ij,t}-d_{j,t},\]
with any prescribed shipment capacities and boundary inventories. A standard linear model minimizes \(\sum_{i,j,t}c_{ij,t}x_{ij,t}\) plus holding and shortage costs. Positive transit times are represented by shifting shipment arrivals to later balance equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plan shipments across several periods while balancing time-varying supplies, demands, inventories, capacities, and costs.
assumptions_latex: The planning horizon is finite and discrete.
Supplies and demands are specified by location and period.
Inventory and shipment variables are nonnegative unless backlogging is explicitly allowed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,I,J)\) is admissible exactly when all period balances, capacities, and boundary conditions hold.

notation.meaning: shipment from supply i to demand j in period t

children.title: Dynamic Inventory
children.top_down_role: Inventory carryover represented through temporal storage structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Inventory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time inventory state equation with optional loss, replenishment, and withdrawal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a location \(v\) and periods \(t=0,\ldots,T-1\), let \(I_{v,t}\) be beginning inventory, \(r_{v,t}\) total replenishment arriving during period \(t\), and \(q_{v,t}\) total withdrawal. With retention factor \(\alpha_{v,t}\in[0,1]\), dynamic inventory obeys
\[I_{v,t+1}=\alpha_{v,t}I_{v,t}+r_{v,t}-q_{v,t}.\]
Feasibility additionally requires prescribed bounds \(\underline I_{v,t}\le I_{v,t}\le\overline I_{v,t}\) and initial inventory \(I_{v,0}\). The lossless case has \(\alpha_{v,t}=1\); backlog models instead permit negative inventory under explicitly stated lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inventory is a time-indexed state obtained from retained stock plus arrivals minus withdrawals, subject to bounds and initial conditions.
assumptions_latex: The horizon is finite and discrete.
Arrivals and withdrawals use a fixed within-period timing convention.
Inventory bounds and initial states are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{v,t+1}=\alpha_{v,t}I_{v,t}+r_{v,t}-q_{v,t}\) with \(\underline I_{v,t}\le I_{v,t}\le\overline I_{v,t}\).

children.title: Transport–Inventory Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interaction between shipment timing and inventory carryover.

knowledge_statements.title: Transport–Inventory Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Node-time balance linking dispatched transport, delayed arrivals, external supply, demand, and inventory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_{a,t}\) be dispatch on arc \(a\) at time \(t\), with transit time \(\tau_a\), and let \(I_{v,t}\) be inventory. The transport and inventory decisions are coupled at every vertex \(v\) and period \(t\) by
\[I_{v,t+1}=I_{v,t}+s_{v,t}-d_{v,t}+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_{a,t+1-\tau_a}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_{a,t},\]
where terms with invalid time indices are zero. Together with arc capacities and inventory bounds, this equality prevents material from being dispatched before it is available and credits incoming transport only upon arrival.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each node and time, next inventory equals current inventory plus supply and delayed arrivals minus demand and dispatches.
assumptions_latex: Time and transit times are integral.
A fixed convention determines whether period events occur before or after inventory measurement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{v,t+1}=I_{v,t}+s_{v,t}-d_{v,t}+\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_{a,t+1-\tau_a}-\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_{a,t}\).

children.title: Terminal-Inventory Regimes
children.top_down_role: Alternative end-horizon requirements for remaining inventory.

knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Inventory Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary conditions distinguishing free, fixed, bounded, cyclic, and penalized terminal stock.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For terminal inventory \(I_{v,T}\), common regimes are: free terminal stock, imposing only \(I_{v,T}\in[\underline I_{v,T},\overline I_{v,T}]\); fixed stock, imposing \(I_{v,T}=\widehat I_v\); depletion, imposing \(I_{v,T}=0\); cyclic stock, imposing \(I_{v,T}=I_{v,0}\); and penalized stock, leaving \(I_{v,T}\) variable but adding a terminal value or penalty \(\phi_v(I_{v,T})\) to the objective. Exactly one declared regime, or a compatible combination of bounds and terminal cost, must be included to determine which end-of-horizon inventories are feasible and how residual stock is valued.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminal stock may be free, fixed, depleted, cyclic, or valued by a terminal cost; the chosen regime closes the finite-horizon model.
assumptions_latex: A finite terminal time \(T\) is fixed.
Terminal bounds and any terminal-value function are specified consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{v,T}\) must satisfy the declared terminal constraint and contributes \(\phi_v(I_{v,T})\) when terminal valuation is used.

notation.meaning: terminal inventory cost or negative salvage value

knowledge_statements.title: Project-Scheduling Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Activity-on-arc acyclic network representation without resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be an acyclic activity-on-arc project network with event vertices, activity durations \(p_a\ge0\), source event \(s\), and completion event \(t\). Event times \(E_v\) are feasible precisely when
\[E_w\ge E_v+p_{(v,w)}\qquad\text{for every }(v,w)\in A,\quad E_s=0.\]
The earliest feasible event times satisfy \(E_w=\max_{(v,w)\in A}(E_v+p_{(v,w)})\), and the minimum project completion time is
\[E_t=\max_{P:s\leadsto t}\sum_{a\in P}p_a.\]
Thus precedence-constrained scheduling without resource limits is represented by a longest-path problem in a directed acyclic network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an acyclic activity network, precedence constraints become difference inequalities and the earliest project completion equals the longest source-to-finish path.
assumptions_latex: The project network is finite and acyclic.
No renewable or cumulative resource constraints are imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_t=\max_{P:s\leadsto t}\sum_{a\in P}p_a\).

notation.meaning: earliest feasible time of event v

children.title: Dynamic Evacuation Flow
children.top_down_role: Temporal network models for moving populations toward designated safe destinations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Evacuation Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time deterministic evacuation with capacities, transit times, and optional storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q_v\ge 0\) be the initial population at each vertex, with \(q_v=0\) outside the source set unless otherwise specified. A dynamic evacuation flow consists of values \(f_a(t)\ge 0\) for every arc \(a\in A\) and admissible departure time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), together with inventories \(z_v(t)\ge 0\). Set \(z_v(-1)=q_v\). For every nonsafe vertex \(v\) and time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\), require \[z_v(t)=z_v(t-1)+\sum_{a=(w,v)}\sum_{s:\,s+\tau_a(s)=t}f_a(s)-\sum_{a=(v,w)}f_a(t).\] Each departure satisfies \(f_a(t)\le u_a(t)\) and \(t+\tau_a(t)\le T\). Flow arriving at a vertex in \(D\) is counted as evacuated and is removed from subsequent conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dynamic evacuation flow moves the initial population through capacitated arcs over time, conserves people and stored inventory at nonsafe vertices, and removes people from the system when they reach safe sinks.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is \(G=(V,A)\), with source set \(S\), safe-sink set \(D\), discrete horizon \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\), capacities \(u_a(t)\), and nonnegative integer transit times \(\tau_a(t)\).
Each vertex has initial population \(q_v\ge0\), and flow may be stored at nonsafe vertices unless a separate waiting restriction is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dynamic evacuation flow is a nonnegative temporal arc flow and inventory process satisfying arc capacities, horizon-admissible travel, temporal conservation at nonsafe vertices, the specified initial population, and absorption at safe sinks.

notation.meaning: flow entering arc a at departure time t
inventory at vertex v after time t

children.title: Dynamic Routing
children.top_down_role: Time-indexed routing choices under temporal capacities or travel times.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic Routing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Route-departure representation of discrete-time evacuation routing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_T\) be the set of admissible route-departure pairs \(r=(P,\theta)\), where the departure time \(\theta\) and the permitted waiting steps determine the time-stamped arc-time pairs used by route \(P\). A dynamic routing assigns \(h_r\ge0\) to every \(r\in\mathcal R_T\). Its induced temporal arc flow is \[f_a(t)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_T:\,(a,t)\in r}h_r.\] The routing is feasible when these induced values respect all arc-time capacities, every used route reaches a safe sink by \(T\), and \(\sum_{r:\,s(r)=s}h_r=q_s\) for every source \(s\in S\). When waiting is allowed, it is represented by time-stamped holdover steps in \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamic routing assigns evacuees to admissible route-and-departure choices whose aggregate arc-time usage respects capacities and evacuates the required amount from each source.
assumptions_latex: The discrete-time temporal network, horizon \(T\), source set \(S\), safe-sink set \(D\), and required source amounts \(q_s\ge0\) are specified.
Every admissible route-departure pair reaches a safe sink by the horizon and respects the applicable waiting policy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A route assignment is feasible precisely when its induced temporal arc flow satisfies the temporal capacity constraints and its source totals equal the required evacuation amounts.

children.title: Evacuation-Time Objectives
children.top_down_role: Completion-time, throughput, or deadline-oriented criteria in evacuation models.

assumptions_latex: A feasible evacuation flow delivers total population \(Q\) to safe sinks.
For each delivered infinitesimal unit or discrete group \(q\), its safe-sink arrival time \(A(q)\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[T_{\mathrm{clear}}=\max_q A(q),\qquad C_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_q A(q),\] with the sum replaced by an integral for continuously divisible flow.

notation.meaning: arrival time at safety of evacuated unit q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two standard deterministic objectives: last-arrival clearance and aggregate arrival time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible evacuation that delivers every unit \(q\) to a safe sink at time \(A(q)\), the clearance-time objective minimizes \(T_{\mathrm{clear}}=\max_q A(q)\), the first time by which the entire population is safe. The aggregate evacuation-time objective minimizes \(C_{\mathrm{sum}}=\sum_q A(q)\) for discrete units, or \(C_{\mathrm{sum}}=\int_0^Q A(\xi)\,d\xi\) for divisible flow indexed by cumulative mass \(\xi\). The objectives are distinct: identical clearance times need not imply identical aggregate arrival times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clearance time measures the last safe arrival, whereas aggregate evacuation time sums or integrates all safe-arrival times.
knowledge_statements.title: Evacuation-Time Objectives

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The entrance-capacity congestion interface requires \(0\le f_a(t)\le u_a(t)\) for every arc \(a\) and departure time \(t\). If congestion is represented by simultaneous occupancy, define \[o_a(t)=\sum_{s:\,s\le t<s+\tau_a(s)} f_a(s).\] Feasibility additionally requires \(o_a(t)\le k_a(t)\) for every \(a,t\). Entrance capacity limits the rate admitted at a time, whereas occupancy capacity limits the total flow concurrently traversing an arc; neither constraint generally implies the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Temporal congestion constraints bound either flow entering an arc at each time or the amount simultaneously occupying it.

children.title: Time-Dependent Transit Times
children.top_down_role: Temporal networks whose traversal duration varies by departure time.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Dependent Transit Times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic discrete-time transit times indexed by departure time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A time-dependent transit-time function assigns a nonnegative integer \(\tau_a(t)\) to every arc \(a=(v,w)\) and departure time \(t\in\{0,\ldots,T\}\). Flow entering \(a\) at time \(t\) reaches \(w\) at \(\alpha_a(t)=t+\tau_a(t)\). The departure is horizon-admissible exactly when \(\alpha_a(t)\le T\), in which case its discrete time-expanded representation is the arc from \((v,t)\) to \((w,\alpha_a(t))\). When FIFO is imposed, it requires \(t\le s\Rightarrow\alpha_a(t)\le\alpha_a(s)\) for all departure times \(t,s\) on the same arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete time-dependent transit time maps each timed arc departure to an integer arrival layer; FIFO additionally prevents a later departure on the same arc from arriving earlier.
assumptions_latex: The time domain is the discrete grid \(\{0,\ldots,T\}\).
Each arc traversal has a deterministic nonnegative integer transit time depending on its departure time, and departures arriving after \(T\) are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A departure on \(a=(v,w)\) at time \(t\) arrives at time \(\alpha_a(t)=t+\tau_a(t)\) and, when \(\alpha_a(t)\le T\), is represented by the corresponding time-expanded arc.

Then there exist a vertex \(k\) on the path and a number \(\delta\) with \(0\le \delta\le \tau\) such that \(P_{ij}\) decomposes as \(P_{ik}\circ P_{kj}\), where \(P_{ik}\) requires at most \(t-\delta\) units of time and \(P_{kj}\) requires at most \(t+\delta\) units of time. The cases \(k=i\) and \(k=j\) are permitted.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A waiting-prohibition regime requires flow arriving at every nonexempt nonsink vertex to depart immediately at that same time. In a time-expanded representation this is enforced by deleting all holdover arcs \(((v,t),(v,t+1))\), or equivalently by imposing \(h_v(t)=0\) for every prohibited vertex-time pair. Temporal conservation then equates flow arriving at \((v,t)\) with flow entering transit arcs departing from \((v,t)\); feasibility may therefore fail even when the corresponding model with unrestricted waiting is feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Waiting Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time temporal walks with vertex-specific or global upper bounds on waiting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have integer arc transit times \(\tau_a\ge 1\) and horizon \(T\). A temporal walk is described by arc-entry times \(t_1,\ldots,t_m\) along a directed walk \(a_i=(v_{i-1},v_i)\), with waiting duration \(w_i=t_{i+1}-(t_i+\tau_{a_i})\) at \(v_i\). Given bounds \(W_v\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\cup\{+\infty\}\), the walk satisfies the vertex-bounded-waiting regime exactly when \(0\le w_i\le W_{v_i}\) for every intermediate visit and \(t_m+\tau_{a_m}\le T\). A global total-waiting regime instead requires \(\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}w_i\le W\). These predicates restrict temporal paths independently of arc-capacity feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A temporal walk is bounded-waiting feasible when every intermediate wait respects its vertex bound, or when its aggregate waiting respects a specified global bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with integral transit times and finite horizon \(T\).
Waiting occurs only at intermediate vertices of a temporal walk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le w_i\le W_{v_i}\) for all intermediate visits, or \(\sum_i w_i\le W\) under the global convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Storage–Waiting Feasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes admissible waiting from feasible storage at intermediate vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a discrete-time dynamic flow, let \(I_v(t)\) denote flow that has reached vertex \(v\) by time \(t\) but has not yet departed. Waiting at \(v\) is storage-feasible precisely when \(0\le I_v(t)\le B_v(t)\) for every permitted storage vertex and time. If storage is prohibited, \(B_v(t)=0\), hence every feasible unit must depart upon availability; if \(B_v(t)>0\), waiting remains possible only while the inventory bound holds. Thus arc-capacity and flow-conservation constraints alone do not certify temporal feasibility when waiting creates positive intermediate inventory: omitting the storage inequalities can admit schedules that exceed physical storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Waiting is feasible exactly while intermediate inventory stays within storage capacity; ignoring this condition can make an arc-feasible temporal schedule physically infeasible.
assumptions_latex: Time is discrete and all arrivals and departures use a common event convention.
\(B_v(t)\ge0\) is the available storage capacity at vertex \(v\) and time \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le I_v(t)\le B_v(t)\) for every storage vertex \(v\) and event time \(t\).

knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Dependent Travel Times
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of fixed-transit-time temporal-network and time-expansion models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose entry at time \(\theta\) onto arc \(a\) incurs travel time \(\tau_a(\theta,x_a)\), where \(x_a\) is the relevant arc inflow, occupancy, or flow history. A fixed time-expanded network uses predetermined arrival arcs from \((u,\theta)\) to \((v,\theta+\bar\tau_a(\theta))\). It represents the model exactly only if the realized travel time equals the predetermined value for every feasible flow. When two feasible flow profiles give different values of \(\tau_a(\theta,x_a)\), no single such expansion represents both profiles. Arrival times and conservation indices then depend on the unknown flow, producing an endogenous, generally nonlinear or equilibrium-constrained model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed time expansion fails when feasible flow profiles induce different arc travel times, because its arrival-time arcs must be chosen before the flow is known.
assumptions_latex: Arc travel time is evaluated from a specified inflow, occupancy, or flow-history state.
The comparison concerns a single fixed time-expanded graph with predetermined temporal arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_a(\theta,x_a^{(1)})\ne\tau_a(\theta,x_a^{(2)})\) for feasible profiles implies that one predetermined arrival arc cannot encode both realizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Multicommodity Temporal Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates splittable temporal multicommodity flow from integral or unsplittable variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For commodities \(k\in K\), a discrete time expansion with exogenous transit times represents splittable temporal flow by variables \(x_{a,t}^k\ge0\), commodity-wise conservation, and shared capacities \(\sum_{k\in K}x_{a,t}^k\le u_a(t)\). This remains a linear multicommodity-flow formulation. The boundary is crossed when each commodity must use one temporal path or its variables must be integral: the additional conditions require path-selection or integrality constraints and are not captured by the continuous relaxation. Moreover, aggregating commodities into one flow is generally invalid when origins, destinations, release times, deadlines, or admissible waiting rules differ, because aggregate conservation does not preserve commodity identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splittable temporal commodities admit a shared-capacity linear model; unsplittability, integrality, or commodity-specific timing prevents reduction to an aggregate single-commodity flow.
assumptions_latex: Transit times and temporal capacities are exogenous on a finite discrete horizon.
Each commodity has specified terminals and temporal requirements.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{k\in K}x_{a,t}^k\le u_a(t)\) yields a linear relaxation, but integral or single-path requirements and heterogeneous temporal data require commodity-indexed constraints.
